[TITLE] Containers should get a /run/user/<UID>/ tmpfs volume mount [BODY] What would you like to be added? Containers should get a /run/user// tmpfs volume mount. Why is this needed? Generally this is needed for conformance with the de facto standard that systemd sets by providing this. Part of this is in FHS, and part in XDG (see below). They provide this feature for the same sorts of reasons that we need it specifically: to store temporary data on a per-user basis with well-known names and not subject to attack via /tmp/ being world-writable (the "sticky" bit is insufficient to fully protect against attacks here). Why bother for Kubernetes? Well, because libraries may want to use /run/user// , and it's much easier to deal with the absence of that directory by just always having that directory. To make that directory's presence universal means that Kubernetes needs to provide it, at least optionally. We've implemented a token cache system that resembles Kerberos credentials caches in that they are kept in temporary storage, preferably tmpfs , but /tmp/ is not an appropriate place (see below) when that code is used on multi-user systems. We want to use temporary storage because we don't want these token caches to survive reboots, for example. Kubernetes pods and containers are not multi-user systems, but libraries that do this sort of caching need to easily support many kinds of environments. Therefore it would be nice to have /run/user// be universally available, so that libraries can use it w/o concern about use on multi-user systems vs. single-user systems. Where /run/user// exists it is created by PAM, but obviously if it were to exist in Kubernetes containers it should be created by Kubernetes. Background: /tmp/ is not appropriate for caches of this sort because on multi-user systems other users can mount attacks on such caches. When coded defensively such attacks can amount to no more than a denial-of-service, but still, it would be easier to safely code such caches if they could use a temporary location that is guaranteed to have the correct permissions ( 0700 ) and where none of the parent directories can have world-writable permissions like 0777 or 01777 . Kerberos client libraries typically use files named /tmp/krb5cc_ , or directories named similarly -- well-known names, not mkstemp() ed names as these need to be easily found without having to look through a possibly-huge directory listing. In Unix time /run/user// is very new, and generally it is only ever created by a PAM, and PAM is not used in starting containers in Kubernetes, therefore /run/user// does not exist in Kubernetes containers. Because such files have to have well-known names, they can be subject to attack on multi-user systems. E.g., creating /tmp/krb5cc_1000 as a symlink to some other file, or creating it as a regular 0666 mode file, etc. Clients need to use O_NOFOLLOW and/or lstat(2) and fstat(2) to make sure that they open only regular, non-symlink files, and they need to check that getuid() owns the file, and that the file has appropriate permissions ( 0600 ). Because we use aud in our tokens to limit their applicability we also have apps that need many tokens. Therefore we want to be able to cache them. Because some of our apps are multi-process apps, or invoke external short-lived programs that fetch and use tokens, we will be able to reduce load on our issuers by having a file-based cache as opposed to in-memory caches only. In our file-based cache of tokens we currently use a 0700 /tmp/tokens_/ , with 0600 regular files in there named after a hash of the issuer and audience of the token modulo the max number of tokens allowed in the cache, and we write the issuer, audience, expiration, token, and other metadata into those files, one token per-file. Ideally we would have /run/user// then we could use /run/user//tokens/ (or some such). (Clearly managing the namespace in /run/user// may eventually be a problem, but at this time it is not, and anyway it won't be a problem for the Kubernetes community to manage.) /run/ is part of the FHS . /run/user// is not part of the FHS, but a) it exists on Linux systems running systemd , b) it is part of XDG and exists on FreeBSD. (I don't have a FreeBSD system to test on, but I think perhaps they use /run/user/${USER}/ rather than /run/user// . Using a UID is better than a username because it's always possible to call getuid() to get the UID, while a username is not always possible or as easy to obtain.)

[TITLE] client library module versioning [BODY] I am well aware of the storied past that kubernetes has had with module versioning, thus I will try and work off the
current state
of the world, but it would be interesting to understand how this impacts old projects virally entangled with
replace
.
If I am developing an internal tool that only imports
k8s.io/client-go/...
and only runs on a cluster that I control, I can trivially pick the exact kubernetes version that I am running,
go get k8s.io/client-go@v0.X.Y
and be happy.
Per
KEP 917
, "consumers are limited to a single copy of kubernetes libraries among all dependencies". As such, if I am running two clusters with different versions and I actually need
v0.20.0
and
v0.21.0
, say due to a feature deprecation, I need to maintain two different versions of my tool?
Taking this a step further, if I maintain a tool that contains a library component and links against the
k8s.io/...
packages, do I need to release separate versions for every kubernetes minor?
Finally, I apologize if this is covered in a document or manual somewhere, but I cannot find it documented anywhere; hence my creation of this issue.

[TITLE] support PreBind for scheduling extender [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Add PreBind and Unreserve verbs to scheduling extender.  The logics of Bind operation could be moved to the Prebind method of extenders. If there are any problem during the prebind/bind stages, the Unreserve method of successful extenders will be called.
Why is this needed?
For now, only one scheduling extender could enable bindVerb and perform binding operations. However, we have multiple extenders which all need to do something, such as updating annotations, just before binding in the bind method.
For example, ExtenderFoo is for extended resource exmaple.com/foo, and ExtenderBar for example.com/bar.
For pods requesting no exmaple.com/foo neither exmaple.com/bar, none of ExtenderFoo/ExtenderBar will be called.
For pods requesting exmaple.com/foo or exmaple.com/bar, ExtenderFoo or ExtenderBar will be called.
BUT if ExtenderFoo and ExtenderBar both needs some operation during Binding, it's NOT possible now， because configuring multiple Bind hooks for extenders is not possible
Furthermore, in our cluster, there are some pods requesting both exmaple.com/foo and exmaple.com/bar.
One possible solution is to rewrite our extenders with scheduling framework. But this needs lots of effort. And some customers use their own schedulers and their schedulers can integrate with our extenders easily, and no need to share the code with them.

[TITLE] The traffic is not routed correctly after the network interface on worker node is restarted [BODY] What happened:
We have a statefulset with 2 replicas, on each pod there is Postgres instance. One acts as master while the other acts as replica.
There are 2 services exposed, one is PG master service and the other is PG replica service. Both services are without selector, and there are 2 endpoints sharing the name of it related service.
The IP of the Postgres pod will be patched into endpoints so that the traffic can be routed to the correct pod when accessing the service.
For example, PG master service is corresponding to the endpoint of the same name, and in that endpoint there is ip of the pod running master Postgres instance.
There is another traffic pod which will set up the DB connection to the master Postgres service.
The problem is:
The traffic pod(issue DB connections with JDBC) and PG master pod are in the same worker node(let’s call it worker1).
The PG replica pod is in another worker(worker2).
Run a testing case which is: “Shutdown network interface on worker1, sleep 60s, take up network interface on worker1”
Then the previous PG replica pod is promoted to master, and the previous PG master pod is demoted to replica.
The traffic pod’s target address is the PG master service name but at that time it connects to the replica pod. Thus the traffic could try to write to a PG in ‘read-only’ mode and test case fails.
The kube-proxy mode is iptables.
We suspect the iptables in kube-proxy doesn’t update the routing information in time. It means the iptables could update the routing information a bit later than the traffic pod establishing the DB connection.
What you expected to happen:
The kube-proxy should route the traffic to correct pod.
How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):
Has been mentioned in "What happened".
Anything else we need to know?:
We made a restart of the kube-proxy and the problem hasn't been reproduced since then. That's strange.
So we hope to know the root cause of that.

[TITLE] Document administration of credentials for system roles/bindings/groups [BODY] The new RBAC documentation includes a section that enumerates the
default roles and role bindings
, which is very helpful. However, it doesn't explain how a component should be configured to actually authenticate as a member of one of these groups.
Specifically, the following auth groups are included in the tables:
system:authenticated
system:unauthenticated
system:masters
system:kube-scheduler
system:kube-controller-manager
system:nodes
system:kube-proxy
(I happen to know that system:authenticated and system:unauthenticated are automatically added to incoming requests as appropriate, but this is never mentioned in the linked document.)
Traditionally, cluster setup tools have not created separate client certificates for all of the core Kubernetes components, but the default cluster roles and cluster role bindings suggest much more granular authentication. The documentation should explain:
The
--authorization-rbac-super-user
option to the API server has been removed and replaced with the system:masters group. How should a user authenticate as a member of this group? Should credentials that place them in that group be created via normal means (e.g. creating a client certificate) or is this membership determined some other way?
How is a given Kubernetes core component or add on determined to be a member of one of these groups? Does each one need its own credentials, or is there some magical way that a components can authenticate as a member of the correct group without configuration? (This is kind of a generalization of the previous bullet point.)
How do the various cluster creation tools (kops, kubeadm, etc.) actually provision credentials for each component?
What are the requirements for creating system component credentials for those of us building clusters from scratch without one of the official tools?
What happens if a system component is
not
configured to be a member of a group that would bind it to the appropriate role? (For example, what happens if the controller manager is started without credentials that assign it the system:kube-controller-manager group? Does it completely fail? And what about the per-control-loop controller manager roles like system:controller:replication-controller? There's no explanation of how to create credentials for the controller manager such that different credentials are used for each control loop. How is this expected to work?)
There are also quite a few cluster roles with the "system" prefix that don't have a default cluster role binding, even though they are clearly intended for a specific component, such as Heapster and the Node Problem Detector. It's not clear how what the cluster administrator is expected to do when installing an add on component that maps to one of these roles/bindings. Is the add on itself supposed to provide instructions on adding appropriate role bindings? If so, why are the roles included by Kubernetes itself and not the add on? This should be explained so cluster administrators know what to expect.
Finally, the use of the "system" prefix on these roles/bindings/groups could be interpreted to mean that they are managed
by
the system, and should never be modified by a cluster administrator. It's not clear if this prefix is just a way of grouping resources that are related to system functionality, or if they're supposed to be "private" (in the sense of a private method in code.) It would be very helpful if the documentation clarified this.
If someone can answer these questions here, I'd be happy to open a PR on the docs repo myself.

[TITLE] Improved support for Pod related Validating Admission Policies. [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Validating Admission Policies is one of my favorite features in kubernetes. I have been using it to write several policies. The most common type of of policies I write are related to PodSpec (most security folks also likely end up doing this). However most of the time I end up writing a policy like the following.
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: "no-gitrepo-volumes"
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
    - apiGroups:   [""]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations:  ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
      resources:   ["pods", "podtemplates", "replicationcontrollers"]
    - apiGroups:   ["apps"]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations:  ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
      resources:   ["deployments", "replicasets", "statefulsets", "daemonsets"]
    - apiGroups:   ["batch"]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations:  ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
      resources:   ["jobs", "cronjobs"]
  validations:
    - expression: |-
        object.kind != 'Pod' ||
        !object.spec.?volumes.orValue([]).exists(v, has(v.gitRepo))
      message: "gitRepo volumes are not allowed."
    - expression: |-
        object.kind != 'PodTemplate' ||
        !object.template.spec.?volumes.orValue([]).exists(v, has(v.gitRepo))
      message: "gitRepo volumes are not allowed."
    - expression: |-
        !['Deployment','ReplicaSet','DaemonSet','StatefulSet','Job', 'ReplicationController'].exists(kind, object.kind == kind) ||
        !object.spec.template.spec.?volumes.orValue([]).exists(v, has(v.gitRepo))
      message: "gitRepo volumes are not allowed."
    - expression: |-
        object.kind != 'CronJob' ||
        !object.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec.?volumes.orValue([]).exists(v, has(v.gitRepo))
      message: "gitRepo volumes are not allowed."
Notice how I have to extract the PodSpec from different object types and so have to write multiple validating expressions. This gets annoying and messy. Could we provide a function or something that extracts the PodSpec from the templates? Then we could write policies like:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: "no-gitrepo-volumes"
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
    - apiGroups:   [""]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations:  ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
      resources:   ["pods", "podtemplates", "replicationcontrollers"]
    - apiGroups:   ["apps"]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations:  ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
      resources:   ["deployments", "replicasets", "statefulsets", "daemonsets"]
    - apiGroups:   ["batch"]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations:  ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
      resources:   ["jobs", "cronjobs"]
  validations:
    - expression: |-
        !extractPodSpec(object).?volumes.orValue([]).exists(v, has(v.gitRepo))
      message: "gitRepo volumes are not allowed."
Why is this needed?
Adding something similar to what I proposed above will greatly help in simplifying policy authoring and therefore reduce the chances of bugs in policies.

[TITLE] --exclude-webhook-validation-ns kube-api option [BODY] What would you like to be added?
--exclude-webhook-validation-ns=kube-system,...
or any similar exclusion as an option in API static Pod
Why is this needed?
It would be more productive that in case we wanted to configure
--enable-admission-plugins
--admission-control-config-file
we have the option to add
--exclude-webhook-validation-ns=kube-system,...
which straight away exempts kube-system and other namespaces we desired to be exempted. This is to help simplify especially when we are in early stage of constructing Image Validation Webhook configurations and the application.
The feature would also ensure that when we change the API static Pod, there is no impact that could lead into it not able to put up because of any mistake in the configurations or validation logics.
Having a global flag like
--exclude-webhook-validation-ns
would simplify the process of ensuring that critical namespaces are exempt from webhook policies. Currently, we must implement namespace-based filtering within each webhook or rely on custom labels/selectors, which can be error-prone and inconsistent across different webhooks.

[TITLE] kubectl logs prints empty output if logs are rotated - some example are wrong [BODY] In many examples we use "kubectl logs" to show container output:
examples/cluster-dns/README.md:$ kubectl logs dns-frontend
examples/downward-api/README.md:$ kubectl logs dapi-test-pod | grep POD_
examples/hazelcast/README.md:$ kubectl logs hazelcast-ulkws hazelcast
examples/mysql-wordpress-pd/README.md:$ kubectl logs mysql
examples/phabricator/README.md:$ kubectl logs phabricator-controller-02qp4
examples/secrets/README.md:$ kubectl logs secret-test-pod
examples/spark/README.md:$ kubectl logs spark-master
Quite often (for me - maybe once every 20-50 executions - I found it by an automated test) "kubectl logs" gives an empty output. The reason is that the docker log file has been rotated in the meantime.
Examples in the current form may be confusing for our users because they will not get the desired output.
The problem affects also our tests for examples, because they will be flaky if we assume we'll get some output form "kubectl logs".

[TITLE] Add a way to control DaemonSet rolling update behavior when DaemonSet pods go non-ready [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Please add a mechanism to control the behaviour of rolling updates when the back-level pods go non-ready.  The current assumption is that any non-ready pod should be immediately restarted at the up-level version.  Some suggestions:
Add a
minTimeBetweenUpgrades
field that sets a minimum time between restarting two pods that are part of the daemonset.
Add a
maxUpgrading
limit that limits how many pods can be upgrading at once.  A pod is not considered "upgraded" until it is "available" at the up-level version.
Why is this needed?
We have a daemonset pod that implements an essential service (pod networking).  Our pod reports readiness for a number of purposes:
It only reports ready once it's in sync with the datastore in order to throttle rolling update.
It only reports ready if it has an active datastore connection.
It only reports ready if the netowrking daemon is ready and able to connect to its peers.
And so on...
In a large cluster, a rolling update can take some time and slowly rolling out minimises load on the API server and minimises network churn.  However, we recently encountered a disruptive roll out at a customer where the following occured:
Rolling update started.
Another component was upgraded in parallel.
The second upgrade caused some of our daemonset pods to go non-ready.
Those daemonset pods immediately got restarted at the new version of the pod.
This caused significant disruption; our daemonset pod is engineered for a cold start like this but restarting all the pods at once results in a lot of handshaking and high load on the API server as everything syncs.

[TITLE] Can we add a quota-scope that can filter by pod status? [BODY] This is a Feature Request
What would you like to be added
Add a quota-scope that can filter by pod status.
Why is this needed
I'm using Volcano to submit a volcano-job, an enhanced job controller. I recently encountered a problem: I submitted a job with N pods. I set the capacity of the volcano-queue to have 5 of them running and the remaining n-5 pods pending. I found that ResourceQuota counted the resources of n pods. When N is large, it is easy to hit the ResourceQuota resource limit, causing my job to fail.
I'm confused by this. I looked in the Kubernetes source code and found that ResourceQuota counts the resources of pending pods. I'm wondering if I can set a scope to exclude pending pods from ResourceQuota.
Unfortunately, when I looked at the ResourceQuota scope, the documentation describes it as determining which resources to include or exclude based on scopes such as "Terminating, NotTerminating, BestEffort, NotBestEffort, PriorityClass, CrossNamespacePodAffinity, VolumeAttributesClass." But there is no way to distinguish the status of the pod.
Comments
I think this is a reasonable requirement. I'm not sure if you agree. Please evaluate it based on my scenario.

[TITLE] [Declarative Validation] Improve Error Reporting for listType=map [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Improve the error reporting for Declarative Validation when validating lists that use listType=map semantics. Currently, validation errors when using listType=map (see:
#130349
) report the list index of the problematic element when it could instead show the key for the field.
Why is this needed?
Declarative Validation uses list indices in its error messages (e.g., spec.conditions[2]: Invalid value). For cases such as listType=map this can make it difficult for users to correlate errors with their configuration, as mapping the index to field might be difficult for a user to derive.
A potentially more user-friendly error message would be to reference the key of the list item, rather than its index. For example, instead of:
spec.conditions[2].status: Invalid value: "Foo": must be "Bar"
the error message might look like:
spec.conditions[name=Ready].status: Invalid value: "Foo": must be "Bar"
This would allow a user to more directly locate the problematic item in their configuration.
This issue originated from a discussion in PR
#130349
, which introduces the Declarative Validation feature:
#130349 (comment)

[TITLE] Automatic fsGroup handling [BODY] What would you like to be added? Note The template for feature requests says: "Feature requests are unlikely to make progress as issues. Please consider engaging with SIGs on slack and mailing lists, instead." I did start a thread on Slack and was asked to create an issue instead. A feature to allow "automatic" handling of fsGroup . Currently users have to pick a number while the actual number often will not matter much. I'd like a feature asking Kubernetes to assign a fsGroup automatically if none has been specified explicitly or e.g. via a webhook/controller/etc. This is part feature request part request for help in figuring out best practices, so I'd also be happy to just have a good discussion. When researching this issue I would have loved to find this exact issue to save me a lot of time. And I do understand (more on that later) that this is partially due to OpenShift specifics and therefore not relevant to this project. /sig node Why is this needed? We need to mount a few ephemeral volumes into a pod/container. These mounts are accessible only to root, meaning the container user (non-root) cannot access them without setting securityContext.fsGroup , which is what we currently do in our operators (set a random fsGroup that is) but this has problems. Background Vanilla Kubernetes requires an fsGroup for non-root container users to access these volumes. OpenShift provides SecurityContextConstraints (SCC), which can automatically assign a valid fsGroup from a specified range if not explicitly set (depending on how exactly they are configured) This helps us avoid specifying an fsGroup directly, which can simplify configuration However, SCCs complicate things as they’re not available in vanilla Kubernetes SCCs can put constraints on the allowed fsGroup values Summary Vanilla Kubernetes requires an explicit fsGroup If not set: Containers fail to access volumes OpenShift behavior will depend on the exact SCC active (it's not possible to find out upfront which is): It might fail if a fsGroup is set and the group is out of the specified range -> Better solution here is to set no fsGroup so OpenShift can assign one automatically It might fail if no fsGroup is set and OpenShift is set up to not assign one automatically This leaves us with no good option. Current Proposed Solution/Idea Note This came out of a longer discussion in #kubernetes-operator on Slack. Detect OpenShift (e.g., by querying the SCC API) If OpenShift: Set a special annotation requiring the restricted-v2 SCC, allowing automatic fsGroup assignment. Don’t set securityContext.fsGroup. Else (vanilla Kubernetes): Hardcode fsGroup. One could argue that this is an OpenShift-specific problem that we’ve addressed. However, I wonder if there’s value in a generalized feature allowing for an automatically assigned fsGroup—without having to specify one manually—when the specific integer id to use is non-essential. Suggestion Leave the current functionality of securityContext.fsGroup as it is: If set to an integer use that If not set, don't set fsGroup at all Add a new value auto that will automatically pick a fsGroup value if none has been set This is just one idea , this could be implemented multiple ways and I do understand that picking the "wrong" group Id might also have security implications

[TITLE] kube-proxy's conntrack flushing of ready=false pods kills valid UDP flows [BODY] What happened?
Setup
single cluster
Pod A talks to Pod B via Service B using the Service's ClusterIP. (Pod B is one of several in a Deployment).
A "connects" to B via UDP (sends an initial message).
kube-proxy on the Node of A sets up DNAT/conntrack/etc to make this work.
B responds on the UDP "connection", possibly multiple times, usually the first within milliseconds, and more following it over the next couple of seconds (the timing isn't important other than it's well below any timeout for the UDP pseuo-connection).
Some time during 5, pod B becomes ready=false via HTTP ready checks.
Expected
The responses of 5 should continue even after 6 happens, as long as pod B is actually healthy.
Actual behavior:
kube-proxy on node A kills the UDP pseudo-connection by clearing the relevant conntrack entry.  This is done here
kubernetes/pkg/proxy/conntrack/cleanup.go
Line 84
      in
2c35d03
if
endpoint
.
IsServing
() {
(and the surrounding code).
Any subsequent messages from pod B are seen to successfully hit node A, but then aren't sent into the pod A's bridge network device (to get the packet into pod A's network namespace).  This is seen with a tcpdump on the Node of A.
Possible fix
Change the condition here
kubernetes/pkg/proxy/conntrack/cleanup.go
Line 84
      in
2c35d03
if
endpoint
.
IsServing
() {
so that ready=false still is "true" for that conditional.  For example, only flush once the pod is actually terminated (no long phase=Running maybe?).
Justification
Pod B needs to be able to go ready=false to load shed when the per pod load is too high.  When it does this, it needs to still process its existing connections.
While the UDP protocol described above maybe seems a bit silly and prone to issues, this is effectively how SIP over UDP works
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3261
and our customers depend upon it so we can't change it.  The client sends an initial
INVITE
request, then the server responds with an immediate
100 Processing
, follow up
180 Ringing
, and finally
200 OK
.  If this problem causes the
200 OK
to be lost then the user's call establishment is disrupted.
Workaround
We put Envoy in place of Pod A and are pointing it at a headless Service that points at Pod B (and it's siblings in its Deployment).  Envoy is configured with very aggressive health checking of the HTTP ready endpoint.  This avoids the DNATing and conntrack dependency on Pod A associated with using a ClusterIP, and so obviously also avoids the problematic kube-proxy behavior that flushes the conntrack entries.
Another workaround is to try to get customers to use SIP over TCP, but not all of them can do this.
What did you expect to happen?
Included above.
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
I think the steps to reproduce are described reasonably well above.  If you want me to spell out a testing approach more specifically I can.
Anything else we need to know?

[TITLE] Separate log and container lifecycle management [BODY] This is a follow-up to issue
#123279
, as the scope of the discussion has expanded beyond the original issue. Therefore, I am opening a new issue to focus on this topic.
In issue
#123279
, the goal was to disable kubelet from removing container logs when the container is deleted. However, disabling kubelet from cleaning up logs of removed containers could introduce potential risks, such as log files consuming excessive disk space, eventually leading to the host running out of storage and becoming unresponsive.
With that in mind, I would like to further discuss a topic we had previously considered:
separating the lifecycle management of containers and their logs in kubelet
, with the retention of logs for deleted containers being a subset of this broader topic.
ref:
kubernetes/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go
Lines 1308 to 1314
      in
af2bf2d
// Remove the container log.
// TODO: Separate log and container lifecycle management.
if
err
:=
m
.
removeContainerLog
(
ctx
,
containerID
);
err
!=
nil
{
return
err
}
// Remove the container.
return
m
.
runtimeService
.
RemoveContainer
(
ctx
,
containerID
)
Below are some features that I think:
Rotation and Compression of Logs from Deleted Pods
: Logs for containers are stored by default under /var/log/pods/, with a unique directory structure based on the pod's namespace-podName-podUUID. Perhaps we should consider compressing the entire pod log directory when the pod is deleted?
Kubelet Management of Deleted Pod Logs
: Kubelet should have a clear configuration to manage the cleanup and retention policy for logs from deleted pods. We could introduce new settings, such as
podLogMaxFiles
and
podLogMaxSize
, similar to the existing containerLogMaxFiles and containerLogMaxSize.
Capacity Limits for Pod Log Directories
: Should we enforce a maximum storage limit for pod log directories? If no limit is set, they could potentially fill up the entire host storage.
I'm not entirely sure if these ideas are on the right track, or if simply disabling kubelet's log cleanup for containers is sufficient. I would greatly appreciate any feedback or suggestions.

[TITLE] scheduler: more fine-grained QHints [BODY] /kind feature
/sig scheduling
/assign
We had a problematic internal feature called
preCheck
(
#110175
).
preCheck prevented us from implementing a fine-grained QHint because it could cause the scenarios like the following:
Node with un-ready taint is created.
Because Node has taint, this
Node/Add
event isn't delivered to QHints because preCheck filters it out.
When Node is ready and the taint is removed, preCheck forwards this Node event to the scheduling queue. However, it's Node/Update (UpdateNodeTaint), not Node/Add.
Plugins that actually want to move Pods via Node/Add couldn't get Node/Add at (2), hence has to subscribe
Node/Update
to catch (3) instead, and handle it like
Node/Add
.
Now, it's disabled finally when QHint is enabled (
#127109
), and we can improve QHints to filter out events more accurately.

[TITLE] podAntiAffinity.preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution of existing Pods is not ignored during scheduling on AKS [BODY] What happened?
According to the documentation (
https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#scheduling-behavior
), any
preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution
rules of existing pods should be ignored during scheduling of new pods. In our AKS cluster, however, the scheduler still takes those preferred anti-affinity weights into account when deciding where to place a new pod.

[TITLE] kube-proxy 1.23 → 1.28+ directly upgrade may introduce Latent failures [BODY] What happened?
We encountered an issue where upgrading kube-proxy
directly
from v1.23 to v1.30 led to a latent failure
that only surfaced a month later.
We’re aware this upgrade path violates the Kubernetes version skew policy and isn’t officially supported. However, the failure mode is subtle and could easily go unnoticed in real-world environments.
Sharing this here to let you decide whether it qualifies as a valid bug worth addressing 😄
From Changelog, In kube-proxy v1.23, KUBE-XLB-* chains were used to handle local traffic masquerading for LoadBalancer-type services. These were renamed to KUBE-EXT-* in v1.24, and mention of KUBE-XLB-* was fully removed starting in v1.28.
What happened:
Initial state: The node was running kube-proxy v1.23, which created KUBE-XLB-* chains. These chains referenced KUBE-SVC-* and KUBE-SEP-* chains.
Upgrade: kube-proxy was upgraded
directly
to v1.30. At this point, both KUBE-XLB-* and KUBE-EXT-* chains existed, but only KUBE-EXT-* was actively used (e.g., referenced by KUBE-NODEPORTS). The node continued to function normally for about a month.
Failure trigger: A pod restarted on the node. This pod was behind a LoadBalancer service with externalTrafficPolicy: Local. During the iptables update (via iptables-restore), kube-proxy failed to run
iptables-restore
due to lingering references from the obsolete KUBE-XLB-* chains. This caused kube-proxy to break
indefinitely
(until a operator go flush the IPTables on node). The error message were obscure：

[TITLE] Allow per-client configuration for rest client backoff manager [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Extend the rest client so the user can provide an optional backoff base / duration when creating the RESTClient.
Why is this needed?
The rest client uses environment variables for configuring the backoff manager for retries on GET requests which error out due to connection reset.  This backoff defaults to 0 if the environment variables are not set (this seems bad).  Also, since the manager depends on environment variables, the defaults are global, so user can't configure them on a per-cluster basis if a process connects to multiple clusters.
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/cbe28cf468c43969d2c170e079f556becfc7adb7/rest/client.go#L124

[TITLE] Allow different orders in OrderedReady podManagementPolicy [BODY] What would you like to be added?
On top of the existing
OrderedReady
policy for a StatefulSet, I'd like to be able to pick minor variants to the order, like a descending rather than ascending order.
Why is this needed?
When the pods in the StatefulSet come with significant state (for example clustered databases where each pod carries its own volume with one shard of the data), there can be significant differences between the first pod and the last, and therefore it can become important to pick in which order they should be deployed. In my case, the older pods (with alphabetically lower names) hold older data, while newer pods have newer data and should ideally come online first. Reversing the ordered followed by the scheduler would allow my workload to become mostly functional again in minutes rather than hours, after a major maintenance such as a kubernetes version upgrade to the node.
I've considered workarounds like
custom schedulers
but they seem overkill and aren't always supported natively by most helm charts out there.
#88362
was withdrawn back in 2020 but it was more about interdependencies between pods.

[TITLE] RelaxedServiceNameValidation feature gate does not cover ingress spec.defaultBackend [BODY] What happened? The RelaxedServiceNameValidation feature gate implementation in allowRelaxedServiceNameValidation() might be incomplete. It checks service names in spec.rules but does not check spec.defaultBackend.service.name . https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/apis/networking/validation/validation.go#L701 This creates inconsistent behavior: Ingresses with relaxed service names in rules can be updated, but those with relaxed names only in defaultBackend cannot. What did you expect to happen? The feature gate should consistently handle relaxed service name validation for both spec.rules and spec.defaultBackend . When the feature gate is disabled, existing Ingresses with RFC 1123-compliant but RFC 1035-noncompliant service names (e.g., "1-default-service") should remain updatable regardless of whether those names appear in rules or defaultBackend . How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Enable RelaxedServiceNameValidation feature gate Create Ingress with defaultBackend with a service name starting with a digit Disable RelaxedServiceNameValidation feature gate Attempt to update this Ingress The update fails because the old service name starts with a digit. Anything else we need to know? Cluster autoscaler is currently in the process of adding cluster limits on dynamic resources, to avoid over-scaling. [TITLE] Event timestamps don't support sub-second precision [BODY] What happened?
We started exporting Kubernetes events into a monitoring system and noticed that some events seem to be out of order (e.g. container started event before container created event). Upon further investigation we concluded that the root cause is the insufficient precision of the event timestamps - the timestamps only support seconds precision - so the order of events which happen in the same second is lost.
This behavior turns out to be by design:
staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/time_proto.go#L45-L48
staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/time_proto.go#L70-L73
It was introduced in commit
5b8a483
.
Given the commit is 5 years old, has it perhaps become obsolete, could it be reverted so that the nanosecond precision is preserved?
What did you expect to happen?
Order of events which happened in the same second is preserved. The relevant timestamps support sub-second precision.
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Query the Kubernetes Events API using client supporting ProtoBuf content type (such
resmoio/kubernetes-event-exporter
, which uses k8s client internally).
Anything else we need to know?

node-status-update-frequency
to
10
seconds by default which may only give the kubelet 4 retry attempts instead of the 5 desired.

All nodes stay
Ready
during a 40 second disconnection/keepalive timeout between the Kubernetes API server (KAS) and etcd resulting in the KAS failing over to another etcd member.

See
#121793
and use a 41 second etcd defrag time to account for a delta amount of time while the Kubernetes components re-establish network connections. While difficult to reproduce outside this simulation, we have had clients report a few problems that appear to confirm this situation may occur.

While resource requests & limits can be added under spec.* that's ignored and not applied.
Proposal
Simply setting pod level resource constraints may not help, and it shouldn't take away the already existing container level constraints. So if the pod can allocate resources according to what the container usage may be over time and can be adjusted, that can work. Would like more suggestions on:

For a pod with multiple set of containers, it may be useful to let the operator adjust what they want over a particular pod and abstract the need of manually configuring container constraints unless needed

[TITLE] SELinux warning controller does not report conflicts with "" [BODY] What happened?
A pod with label
:::s0:c0,c2
should conflicts with a pod with label
:::
(or
""
).
Kubelet defaults the first three components of the label to
system_u:object_r:container_file_t:s0:c0,c2
/
system_u:object_r:container_file_t:
and these are two different labels. If the pods have
spec.securityContext.seLinuxChangePolicy: MountOption
, kubelet correctly reports the conflict + refuses to run the second pod with something like:
Unable to attach or mount volumes: unmounted volumes=[vol], unattached volumes=[], failed to process volumes=[vol]: conflicting SELinux labels of volume pvc-3f62d9ae-7ad0-47d4-8b5a-72656ace42e6: "system_u:object_r:container_file_t:s0:c0,c2" and ""
However, the SELinux warning controller does not report any conflict and it should.
What did you expect to happen?
SELinux warning controller should emit something like:
SELinuxLabel "" conflicts with pod testpod-c2 that uses the same volume as this pod with SELinuxLabel ":::s0:c0,c2". If both pods land on the same node, only one of them may access the volume.
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Run two pods, one with
spec.securityContext.seLinuxOptions.level = "s0:c0,c2"
and the second one with
nil

Summary (to be transcribed into a doc):
Apply conceptually is intended to enable users to just specify a configuration and "make it so". But it's not that easy.
We represent default values explicitly in the API so that system components, ecosystem components, tools, and users don't need to reason about implicit behaviors, especially since such behaviors can change across API versions.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/devel/api-conventions.md#defaulting
We also want apply to work with automation, such as auto-scaling, and asynchronously filled-in values, such as node or IP assignments.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/devel/api-conventions.md#late-initialization
Therefore, unspecified values are (supposed to be) interpreted by apply as not managed by the user.
To do this, apply is implemented as a kind of 3-way merge, of their previous configuration, their new configuration, and the live state in apiserver/etcd. Obviously, this means that the previous configuration needs to be stored somewhere. It is currently stored in an annotation on each resource (
#16543
).
The diff-and-patch process has a few tricky issues. One is that we often don't want to overwrite arrays, which is standard json patch behavior, and we don't want to merge elements positionally, either. Many arrays have primary keys, similar to maps. We created a custom patch strategy to implement this behavior:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/devel/api-conventions.md#strategic-merge-patch
One problem we haven't solved yet is that OneOf / union cases also need to be recognized, so that the previous value can be automatically nulled when a selection is changed (example of a OneOf issue:
#24198
).
We need to find a way to represent the merge strategy, merge keys, and OneOf relationships in Swagger (probably Swagger 2.0), as well. Otherwise, kubectl apply won't work properly with a cluster of a different release.
We need to clean up all cases in the API types.go files that don't properly allow us to distinguish unspecified values from default values (e.g., using pointers for optional fields).
We should ensure imperative mutations like scale, label, and annotate don't update the last-applied-configuration annotation by default, since that would cause those changes to get removed on the next apply if not added to the user's configuration file.
The user needs to be able to explicitly nil values when performing apply (so that needs to be fixed if it doesn't work).
We should detect conflicts between the live state and the applied state (
#13576
).
We should fix the handling of secret data (
#23564
,
#20508
).
We need a pattern to recommend for rolling out ConfigMaps (
#22368
). (I
think
changing the name of the ConfigMap should just work, once we have server-side cascading deletion.)
We should figure out how to automatically test apply
#26234
.
Search issues for "kubectl apply" to find other misc. bugs and features.

[TITLE] Align Ratcheting behavior for "atomic" data type between Built-ins and CRDs [BODY] What would you like to be added?
The updated
KEP-5073
proposes a user-experience-focused approach for ratcheting
structType=atomic
and
mapType=atomic
collections in built-in types. Specifically, it suggests that re-validation during an update should only occur for the sub-fields or key-value pairs that have actually changed, rather than re-validating the entire atomic collection if any part is modified.
This behavior differs from the current, stricter interpretation for atomic collections in CRDs under
KEP-4008
.
Proposal
Built-in Types
: Solidify the decision for this granular ratcheting behavior (only revalidating changed parts) for structType=atomic and mapType=atomic in built-in types as per KEP-5073.
CRD
: Align the ratcheting behavior for
structType=atomic
and
mapType=atomic
in CRDs (KEP-4008) so that CRDs also adopt this more granular, user-experience-focused approach of only revalidating the changed sub-fields or key-value pairs within atomic collections, ensuring consistency across built-in types and CRDs.
Why is this needed?
Aligning the ratcheting behavior for atomic structs and maps across built-in types and CRDs is needed to:
Provide a uniform and predictable validation ratcheting experience for users.
Uphold the core principle of minimizing update rejections due to validation failures on fields or map entries that were not modified by the user, even as "atomic".
Clearly distinguish the "atomic" nature for ownership purposes from the granularity of re-validation during ratcheting.

[TITLE] kubectl debug --copy-to option copy or add labels [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Add an option to kubectl debug --copy-to to either on the fly add labels to the clone or copy the existing labels from the origin.

kubectl debug --copy-to
currently does not copy labels. I reckon there is a good reason for it. (Probably if a pod from a replica-set gets cloned and would be removed again because of
pod-template-hash
).
However without labels the debug pod without labels is pretty much useless in a cluster which has networkpolicies based on labels if you actually want to debug network stuff.
Happy to contribute a pr if I am not the only one thinking there should be an option to label the pod (or copy labels).

[TITLE] Cluster Scoped LimitRanges [BODY] What would you like to be added?
I want to be able to have 1 LimitRange for my entire cluster.
Why is this needed?
We have jobs that need an unknown amount of resources and in namespaces that are automatically created.
I'd rather have 1 resource floor for all pods cluster wide preventing issues with scheduling

[TITLE] App container is started before initContainers could complete on node reboot [BODY] What happened?
On node reboot, we see app container is started before initContainers could complete. Essentially both app and initContainers are running in parallel. We are using initContainers to ensure dependent drivers are loaded by other pod before the app container could start. But because app container is starting in parallel, they hit a failure. This was not seen with k8s 1.27 and only happening with 1.28. Also, this happens only on node reboot, not during fresh install of our application (gpu-operator)

[TITLE] StructuredAuthentication - remove the hard limit on JWTAuthenticators [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Hi folks,
I was recently reading through the
Structured Authentication KEP
and I find it very exiting. I was wondering how many authenticators could be configured and my first guess would have been that there would be no in code limitation. I found out that there is
a comment
in the code that says that this number will be 64 for some future release of Kubernetes. The reasoning behind this comment seems to be
another comment
made during PR review. That comment references the
Structured Authorization KEP
and the limit of 64 that is applied to lists, however in the KEP the limit is only mentioned for the number of
matchConditions
which I think makes sense. Also in the current version of the validation for AuthorizationConfiguration there seems to be
no limit
for the number of authorizers.
Would you reconsider not enforcing the hard limit of 64 for the number of JWTAuthenticatiors?
kind ping
@aramase
as author and
@enj
as reviewer of the mentioned PR
Why is this needed?
I understand that having > 64 authenticators is probably not the most common use case, however there are scenarios in which this is useful, i.e. a single kubernetes cluster is accessed by multiple external systems (ex. CI systems, other k8s clusters, etc) and this access is granted because that central k8s cluster has all of these external systems trusted via JWTAuthenticator configurations.

[TITLE] Job readiness gates [BODY] What would you like to be added?
An alternative to
Job.spec.suspend
that allows multiple controllers to cooperate towards starting a Job.
This is analogous to scheduling gates
https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-scheduling-readiness/
Why is this needed?
This would enable queueing of steps of a workflow.
For example, the job could have:
readinessGates:
  - kueue.k8s.io/suspend
  - snakemake.io/step
The job is only allowed to run (create pods) if all gates are removed.
In the case above,
snakemake.io/step
would be removed by snakemake when all the dependencies for this job are completed.
At this point, kueue would allow this job to compete for resources in the queue. When there is enough quota to run this job, Kueue would remove the
kueue.k8s.io/suspend
.

[TITLE] Garbage collector for container images is unpredictable and inconsistent [BODY] What happened?
The garbage collector for container image lifecycle does not seem to adhere to the documentation and the provided parameters.
From
the docs
,
the configured HighThresholdPercent value triggers garbage collection, which deletes images in order based on the last time they were used, starting with the oldest first. The kubelet deletes images until disk usage reaches the LowThresholdPercent value.
From some tests, this does not appear to be the case. Often, the GC will delete way more images than requires, often dropping below
LowThresholdPercent
and deleting 3 to 4 at a time.
What did you expect to happen?
The GC should delete images until
LowThresholdPercent
is reached.
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Either create some dummy images (we created a set of images with increasing sizes, but any will do the job), or identify some appropriate image already available on Docker Hub.
For each image, deploy a pod and then delete it. The image will remain in the cache.
After a while, the disk space will reach the
LowThresholdPercent
first and
HighThresholdPercent
later. The GC will be triggered.
The GC should in theory delete the earliest unused image. This does not always happen: priority is sometimes given to other images, or more than one is deleted, in a seemingly random order.
Anything else we need to know?
The bug is hard to reproduce and needs some trial and error. Sometimes, images are correctly deleted in order and one at a time, other times the behaviour is apparently random.
If this behaviour is expected, then the docs should be appropriately corrected to mention the choices the GC makes. This is important as I/O spikes in the GC may cause SLA issues in other services deployed in the node.

[TITLE] strict golangci-lint [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Let's use this issue to discuss how to proceed with
strict linting in Kubernetes
.
For each issue found by
hack/verify-golangci-lint.sh -s
(for "strict") we need to decide how severe it is:
ignore it completely, i.e. disable the check = 👎
merely point it out in new code, but don't prevent merging = 👀
merge-blocking = 👍
should be fixed in existing code = 🚀
I am going to summarize the different issues in separate comments below, sorted by linter. For each comment, vote with reactions. I am using the first issue that gets reported, so this is not necessarily representative. See
this gist
for the full output.
Remember that intentional exceptions are okay (
// nolint:<something>
), so let's not disable a check just because it didn't make sense for that particular example. One occurrence of a real bug in production code may make a check worthwhile.
There's no need to vote on all issues. When there's no clear opinion either way, the default will be "merge-blocking".
This was presented at KubeCon (see
https://kcseu2023.sched.com/event/1LXBP/improving-code-quality-enabling-additional-linters
, which was recorded) and it seems useful to gather opinions here, so let's start voting. We may have Prow support for GitHub annotations by middle of May or at least will know how much longer that might take, so let's keep this open for a month and then revisit the topic.
Why is this needed?
Improve the quality of Kubernetes code.

[TITLE] Support scheduling hint in Pod.Spec to have sticky scheduling [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Provide a mechanism to hint the scheduler to schedule a pod, which is to be created, to a node where the pod's owner controller believe it's optimal to schedule that specific pod to that node.
Why is this needed?
Some batch workloads have checkpoints saved in local storage, although they can restore checkpoints from previous node's storage via network, the network overhead is non-trivial. This is common in using IndexedJob or JobSet. When there is a disruption, Pods are recreated and users have to implement mechanisms outside k8s to workaround this problem or have suboptimal performance.
Currently,
pod.status.nominatedNodeName
achieves similar logic with one drawback: the
pod.status
field can't be initialized at pod creation so pod controllers can't really rely on it otherwise race conditions may happen.

[TITLE] Soft eviction of pods with long grace periods blocks hard evictions when under resource pressure [BODY] What happened?
When kubelet detects that it's under resource pressure, it first attempts to do soft evictions, until the hard eviction threshold is reached. When a pod is soft-evicted, it respects the configured max pod grace period seconds, and until the pod has shut down, kubelet will not attempt to soft OR hard evict another pod, even if the hard eviction threshold is reached.
As a result, one pod taking a long time to shut down can cause kubelet to run out of resources. From
this comment
and
this comment
this behavior seems to be by design
In our case, we saw one soft eviction take 7 hours to complete, and meanwhile, resources usage kept climbing without any automation trying to save the node. Had other pods gotten soft evicted while this pod shut down, this would not be an issue. Manual intervention prevented it from reaching hard-eviction thresholds, but had that not happened, this would have entirely exhausted the node with no automated action
What did you expect to happen?
I would expect that kubelet would keep trying to soft evict other pods if one is taking a long time to shut down. Or at the very least, start hard evicting pods if the hard eviction threshold is reached. It could also hard-evict the pod that was soft-evicted but is taking a long time to shut down.
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Create two pods that get scheduled to the same node that have emptyDir volumes and a prestop hook that just sleeps forever
Start filling up those emptyDir volumes with
dd
until soft eviction threshold is reached
Watch as kubelet soft-evicts one pod
Continue filling up the emptyDir volumes with
dd
Kubelet will not evict (hard or soft) even as the resource is totally exhausted

[TITLE] Support for Topology Aware Routing in winkernel proxier [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Topology Aware Routing was introduced in
#99522
and at the time of introduction it was introduced for
iptable
and
ipvs
proxiers. The feature is in beta since 1.23 but support is missing for Windows worker nodes.
Why is this needed?
Windows worker nodes are supported by various distributions and cloud providers. A lot of them already automatically set
topology.kubernetes.io/zone
based on the service provider's availability zone information for these nodes. if you have a multi-zone environment with Windows worker nodes, it is not possible to benefit from Topology Aware Routing, therefore all the benefits highlighted in
https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-network/2433-topology-aware-hints
are missed. If the cluster has active Linux workloads in these zones, interacting with these services through Windows workload may actually turn out to be costly - both performance & bandwidth wise.
It looks like there may not be a technical blockers (HNS, for eg) to have this. Today all the endpoint registration logic in winkernel proxier resides in
syncProxyRules
where iTP, eTP policies are evaluated - this diverges from iptables, ipvs proxiers that have evolved to use
CategorizeEndpoints
from
topology.go
for this purpose, which also handles selection of endpoints matching node's topology zone.
If there are technical reasons for this not being supported, the lack of support should be documented and tracked.

[TITLE] CVE-2025-4563: Nodes can bypass dynamic resource allocation authorization checks [BODY] CVSS Rating:
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L
-
Low
(2.7)
A vulnerability exists in the NodeRestriction admission controller where nodes can bypass dynamic resource allocation authorization checks. When the DynamicResourceAllocation feature gate is enabled, the controller properly validates resource claim statuses during pod status updates but fails to perform equivalent validation during pod creation. This allows a compromised node to create mirror pods that access unauthorized dynamic resources, potentially leading to privilege escalation. In practice, sanity checks in the kubelet prevent starting those mirror pods after they have been created. Even if they were started, an attacker probably already has gained full access to the node and with most dynamic resources won’t be able to gain additional privileges.
Am I vulnerable?
All clusters that are using the DynamicResourceAllocation feature (disabled by default) and static pods together may be vulnerable.
Affected Versions
kube-apiserver: v1.32.0 - v1.32.5
kube-apiserver: v1.33.0 - 1.33.1
How do I mitigate this vulnerability?
This issue can be mitigated by:
If you're not actively using the DynamicResourceAllocation features, the safest and simplest action is to turn off the feature on the API server.
Fixed Versions
kube-apiserver >= v1.32.6
kube-apiserver >= v1.33.2
Detection
All clusters that are using the DynamicResourceAllocation feature and static pods may be vulnerable.  Run the following command to see if the feature is in use:
kubectl get ResourceClaim --all-namespaces
and
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r ' .items[]  | select(.metadata.annotations["kubernetes.io/config.mirror"] == "true")  | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"'

[TITLE] Coordinated Leader Election [BODY] What would you like to be added?
A component leader election mechanism that is safer for upgrades and rollbacks. This can be done by making two
key modifications:
Instead of a race by component instances to claim the lease, component instances
declare candidacy for a lease and a election coordinator claims the lease for the
best available candidate. This allows the election coordinator to pick a
candidate with the lowest version to ensure that skew rules are not violated.
The election coordinator can mark a lease as "end of term" to signal to the
current leader to stop renewing the lease. This allows the election
coordinator to preempt the current leader and replace it with a better one.
Why is this needed?
Today, node-by-node upgrades, as used by CAPI, kubeadm and similar violate Kubernetes skew policies because of the component leader elections behave.

[TITLE] Enhance Egress Configuration for Finer Grain Control Over APIService and Webhook traffic [BODY] What would you like to be added?
The hypershift project would love to see the ability to control at a finer level what traffic goes through this component in the egress config as well.
The environment to think about is a split control plane/data plane environment where a set of webhooks/apiservices are in a colocated network with the kube-apiserver (and therefore have direct IP connectivity to those webhooks/apiservices. However: there are a subset of "in cluster/data plane" apiservices/webhooks that will need to proxy through konnectivity in order to hit the appropriate endpoint (in cluster services like metrics apiservice, in cluster webhooks like istio, etc).
Right now it's an all or nothing approach for specifying if webhook and apiservice traffic goes through konnectivity or direct. To work around this: a user has to deploy agents in both the "control plane network" that advertise the set of ips for the webhook traffic and then traffic has to go kube-apiserver -> konnectivity server -> konnectivity agent -> webhook backend even though it can optimally go kube-apiserver -> webhook backend
Current workaround is the konnectivity agents in the control plane network advertises the "subset" of ips that exist in the control plane: and then the suite of konnectivity agents deployed in the cluster advertise a "default route" for all other ips.
Considerations:
Typically in these modes a "provider" will be in control of services within the same network as the Kube-Apiserver (providers that provide a managed Kubernetes service). Therefore I think the definition of services within that network should be controlled by the configuration file fed to the Kubernetes APIServer versus something "dynamic" a client could do to a APIService or webhook (like a label, etc). I think it would be safe to assume that if it is not in that explicit "allowlist" then it could proceed to be processed by Konnectivity and the associated system.
General things to consider:
How would a possible "allow list" look like?
What current data does the kube-apiserver have context wise before calling a webhook/apiservice (which then is processed by the egress config?
How can that be processed against a egress config and ultimately make a decision to "send direct" or "send through the proxy"?
In case it helps to know the work around typically used today: APIServices typically point to a "Service within the cluster" that is a "headless" service with no actual endpoint IP. An endpoint IP is defined to the "VIP" that fronts that APIService in the control plane network. Once there: the Kube-Apiserver looks up that endpoint IP and issues the request to konnectivity based off that VIP. A konnectivity-agent in the control-plane network advertises that it is the specific agent to process traffic for that IP. It is proxied to that agent within the same control plane network which then ultimately just sends the traffic to that VIP. All traffic not to that explicit list of VIPs goes to konnectivity-agents in the cluster that advertise a "default route" meaning process all traffic not destined to agents advertising specific IPs. Default route agents all live in the "data plane" network that is separate from the control plane network
Why is this needed?
Allows finer grained control of KAS egress traffic.

[TITLE] New feature to allocate specific devices using DRA - usecase and design proposal [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Feature to allocate a specific device to a Pod using webhook to generate appropriate DRA resources from user's intention in Pod manifest.
Steps
User appends node name and device ID (PCI address) to
.metadata.annotation
to Pod manifest
Webhook converts the designation in
.metadata.annotation
into a set of resource claim and resource claim template
DRA resource controller schedules the Pod to the designated node
DRA driver allocates the designated device to the container(s) of the Pod
Why is this needed?
Allocating a specific device to a Pod is meaningful in the following usecases.
Efficient device allocation:
allocate an AI device which is located near a NIC on a PCI-Express bus to accelerate RDMA (e.g.,
AI Device 2
is better for apps running both on
Node1
and
Node 2
in the picture below) - this can also be used by some automated tool to schedule Pods to the best location with certain cards w.r.t. co-working Pods
Debugging:
allocate an unhealthy AI device to a debug-purpose Pod
In the current Kubernetes architecture, several challenges exist for the usecases.
With classic device plugin, no parameters like device ID can be specified in Pod manifest
With DRA, parameters can be defined in device class parameters and claim parameters, and therefore we need some additional mechanism if user wants to specify per-Pod parameters

[TITLE] Kubernetes.io website has insufficient visual indication that there's content if the user scrolls down [BODY] I myself didn't know for the longest time that there's more content below the fold, and I can bet you many other users would completely miss most of the content on the main page as well.
I've seen other websites with a similar design (e.g. Google Drive) have a conspicuous down-arrow. Alternately have some of the content that's down below peak a little above the fold. There should be some indication that there's more content down there.

could
see the volumes with

as translated to CSI already.

To remove unnecessary code in scheduler.

[TITLE] csi-translation-lib: Support structured and contextual logging [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Migrate to use structured logging and contextual logging in csi-translation-lib.
Why is this needed?
CSI Sidecar is advancing its support for structured logging and contextual logging. Therefore we need to implement support for structured logging and contextual logging in csi-translation-lib too, which is used internally by CSI Sidecar.

)

New repo (kubernetes/mungedocs)
Into kubernetes.github.io directly
Into kubernetes/contrib. This is my least favorite of the options since contrib is currently a general purpose dumping ground.

[TITLE] CVE-2025-24514: ingress-nginx controller configuration injection via unsanitized auth-url annotation [BODY] CVSS Rating:
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H
(Score: 8.8, High)
A security issue was discovered in
ingress-nginx
where the `auth-url` Ingress annotation can be used to inject configuration into nginx. This can lead to arbitrary code execution in the context of the ingress-nginx controller, and disclosure of Secrets accessible to the controller. (Note that in the default installation, the controller can access all Secrets cluster-wide.)
Am I vulnerable?
This issue affects ingress-nginx. If you do not have ingress-nginx installed on your cluster, you are not affected. You can check this by running `kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --selector app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx`.
This issue does not affect you if you have the `enable-annotation-validation` CLI argument enabled. (This option is enabled by default starting from ingress-nginx v1.12.0.)
Affected Versions
< v1.11.0
v1.11.0 - 1.11.4
v1.12.0
How do I mitigate this vulnerability?
ACTION REQUIRED:
The following steps must be taken to mitigate this vulnerability: Upgrade ingress-nginx to v1.11.5, v1.12.1, or any later version.
Prior to upgrading, this vulnerability can be mitigated by setting the `enable-annotation-validation` CLI argument to “true”.
Fixed Versions
ingress-nginx
main@ab470eb
To upgrade, refer to the documentation:
Upgrading Ingress-nginx
Detection
Suspicious data within the `auth-url` annotation of an Ingress resource could indicate an attempt to exploit this vulnerability.
If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact
security@kubernetes.io
Acknowledgements
This vulnerability was reported by Nir Ohfeld, Ronen Shustin and Sagi Tzadik from Wiz
The issue was fixed and coordinated by Marco Ebert, James Strong, Tabitha Sable, and the Kubernetes Security Response Committee

[TITLE] [Proposal]  Add most non-deprecated flags to the Kubelet configuration API [BODY] Proposal:
Add most non-deprecated flags to the Kubelet configuration API. These will still be settable via flag (flag values override config values).
Background:
The decision of which Kubelet flags to expose in the Kubelet configuration was historically tied to the Dynamic Kubelet Configuration feature. Specifically, the configuration was designed to be shared across nodes. Dynamic Kubelet Configuration has since been deprecated and removed, and this concern is no longer relevant
Motivation:
Consolidating more of the configuration into the configuration API will let users manage their Kubelet configuration via a single API surface, rather than needing to split the configuration across flags and a configuration file.
Add:
HostnameOverride
NodeIP
config.ContainerRuntimeOptions (except deprecated PodSandboxImage)
RuntimeCgroups
ImageCredentialProviderConfigFile
ImageCredentialProviderBinDir
CertDirectory
RootDirectory
WindowsService
WindowsPriorityClass
CloudProvider - note: this may turn into a boolean option
Open Question: "alpha" flags
These flags claim to be alpha (
<Warning: Alpha feature>
), but appear to be ungated. These should probably be treated as default-GA, and added to the config.
NodeLabels
LockFilePath
ExitOnLockContention
The following options will remain flag only:
KubeConfig, BootstrapKubeConfig - We could consider adding these, but it seems odd to point one config file at the other.
KubeletConfigFile, KubeletDropinConfigDirectory - Point to the Kubelet config (don't want a circular reference!)
Deprecated flags:
MinimumGCAge
MaxPerPodContainerCount
MaxContainerCount
RegisterSchedulable
KeepTerminatedPodVolumes
ExperimentalMounterPath
ExperimentalNodeAllocatableIgnoreEvictionThreshold
CloudConfigFile
PodSandboxImage
azure-container-registry-config
cAdvisor flags - Accidental flag leak
version flag / help flag - Not config
logging flags - Relevant fields are already included in the logging configuration
Historical References:
#40117
- Flags that can't be shared across nodes are moved out of shared config type (removed Hostname, NodeIP)
#44061
- Extract CROptions from KubeletConfig
#46254
- Removed CertDirectory, RootDirectory, CloudProvider

[TITLE] Support objectSelector filtering for Webhooks on CONNECT Operations (e.g., pods/exec) [BODY] What would you like to be added? Enable support for the objectSelector field in ValidatingWebhookConfiguration for webhooks that handle CONNECT operations, such as pods/exec . This would allow webhook invocations to be filtered based on pod labels, similar to how objectSelector works for CREATE and other operations. Why is this needed? We are currently using a ValidatingAdmissionWebhook to intercept CONNECT operations (e.g., pods/exec ) across the entire cluster. However, this broad scope is inefficient and introduces unnecessary overhead. We want to scope the webhook to only target specific pods based on labels, reducing impact and avoiding unintended side effects in case the webhook pods are down. For example, if the webhook pods are unavailable, all pods/exec operations throughout the cluster are blocked; effectively making the entire cluster inaccessible for interactive debugging or remote command execution. While the objectSelector field works as expected for CREATE operations, it appears to be unsupported or non-functional for CONNECT operations. For example, using the following configuration causes the webhook not to trigger at all, even for matching pods: objectSelector : matchLabels : controller.devfile.io/creator : " foo " It is currently documented that resources that cannot have labels are not supported for matching https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/extensible-admission-controllers/#matching-requests-objectselector This issue has been previously discussed in: Propagate pods labels to pods/exec subresource to filter objects on webhooks config side #91732 – originally raised but closed due to inactivity Webhooks don’t get triggered for pods/exec when objectSelector is used #132287 – related discussion on webhook filtering limitations, where I got feedback to use namespaceSelector Actually, namespaceSelector does not help in our scenario, as our workloads often share namespaces. We require pod-level granularity, which only objectSelector can provide. Supporting objectSelector for CONNECT operations would bring consistency to webhook behavior and allow for more precise and efficient admission control logic. If there is an alternative way to achieve this targeted behavior, we would appreciate any guidance.

[TITLE] Generate static, object-focused documentation of types [BODY] Users should not have to read our go code to get documentation of the API types.  They could use swagger-ui.  But the swagger-ui is also not a good presentation because:
It presents too much info about REST that is not relevant to most users:
it talks about POST, etc.  However, people are mostly going to use either Kubectl or pkg/client.  Those don't use the word POST.  Kubectl uses "create" and pkg/client uses "Create()".
it talks about the URLs.  However several parts of the url (api version, namespace) are not things that users normally need to think about when they are using Kubectl.  Mostly they just want to know what fields can be used and what they mean.
you have to click several times to find the schema on the swagger-ui page.
It is not as accessible as markdown documentation
I don't think that the swagger-ui schema blurbs will be indexed in same way that github.com markdown docs are.
is is a different style than the markdown docs.
swagger inlines all subtypes in each object's schema.  This makes the schema overwhelming and defeats the grouping of related things that can be ignored as a group like SecurityContext or various volume plugins.  I'd rather there were links to subobjects.
Therefore, we should generate markdown docs for the API types (but not the REST endpoints).
We could maybe generate this using a go program that reflects the struct tags from all the types in pkg/api/v1/types.go.

[TITLE] CVE-2025-1767: GitRepo Volume Inadvertent Local Repository Access [BODY] Issue Details
A security vulnerability was discovered in Kubernetes that could allow a user with create pod permission to exploit gitRepo volumes to access local git repositories belonging to other pods on the same node.
This issue has been rated Medium (
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N
) (score: 6.5), and assigned
CVE-2025-1767
.
Am I vulnerable?
This CVE only affects Kubernetes clusters that utilize the in-tree gitRepo volume to clone git repositories from other pods within the same node. Since the in-tree gitRepo volume feature has been deprecated and will not receive security updates upstream, any cluster still using this feature remains vulnerable.
Affected Components
kubelet
Affected Versions
All versions of Kubernetes
How do I mitigate this vulnerability?
To mitigate this vulnerability, you must use an init container to perform git clone operation and then mount the directory into the Pod's container. An example of this approach is provided
here
.
Note: You can also restrict the use of gitRepo volumes in your cluster using policies such as ValidatingAdmissionPolicy or through Restricted pod security standard policy. You can use the following Common Expression Language (CEL) expression as part of a policy to reject use of gitRepo volumes:
has(object.spec.volumes) || !object.spec.volumes.exists(v, has(v.gitRepo))
Detection
To detect whether this vulnerability has been exploited, you can use the following command to list all pods that use the in-tree gitRepo volume and clones to a .git subdirectory.
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.volumes[].gitRepo.repository | test("^/")) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, repository: (.spec.volumes[] | select(.gitRepo) | .gitRepo.repository)}'
If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact
security@kubernetes.io
Acknowledgements
This vulnerability was reported by Christophe Hauquiert.

[TITLE] Gracefull and Controlled / Ordered Cluster Shutdown and Controlled / Ordered Startup [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Could we get some sort of technology to get an organized and controller "complete cluster shutdown" and "controlled startup" into Kubernetes?
Background - Shutdown:
From time to time we need to poweroff a data-center i.e. for maintenance purposes. In case we have a single cluster in a single data-center with some workload on top of it - we need to controll the shutdown of the workload (scale to replicas = 0) before we can drain and shutdown all the workers and control plane in a given kubernetes cluster.
We do not want to delete the whole cluster during this exercise as re-deploment of cluster and workload would be a lot of traffic and load.
Background - Startup:
When we start up the cluster and its nodes - the workload needs to be re-scheduled (scale to replicas >0) once a specific number of workers is back alive in the cluster and ideally to the same number of replicas as "before" the shutdown. So we need some sort of control on how long the "scale up" should wait before the workload gets started to avoid imbalance - and re-balance needs during power-on / startup.
I understand that we basically never want to shutdown a whole cluster - but sometimes / due to physical maintenace or maintenance on the platform - it might still be required.. also physical re-locations need this as well.
Idea would be some sort of automation / controller based process that would scale down everything to 0 while remembering the scale "before shutdown" - and during power-on - scale back to what we had before but in relation to wait for a set of workers and / or wait for some sort of timeout.
Why is this needed?
Physical maintenance needs - maintenance needs that require a full rack ... full data-center to be powered off.

.
