[TITLE] Pending image downloads of deleted containers are never interrupted, leading to possible DoS [BODY] What happened?
During a research project on Kubernetes, we discovered a potential bug on any reasonably recent Kubernetes version (we tested in 1.25 to 1.29) that affects all clusters regardless of the container runtime used. By exploiting the fact that the CRI-API does not maintain the container download status, we created a denial of service via resource exhaustion.
When an user deploys a pod, the deployed container(s) may rely on image(s) that are not present on the target node, triggering a download by the container runtime. However, if that pod is deleted (either with or without the
--force
flag) before the container runtime completes the download of the image, this download will be carried on anyway. Kubernetes tracks no information at all about the download, and there is no way of interrupting it unless the container runtime is forcibly terminated and recreated.
This (useless, as the images will never be used) sequence of downloads will waste the node’s CPU and network bandwidth and block the download queue, preventing the deployment of other containers with images yet to be downloaded. We experimented on a wide variety of settings, including but not limited to private clouds, public clouds and edge devices, with different container runtimes (containerd and CRI-O) and different Kubernetes providers (kubeadm, microk8s, and GKE).
The impact this bug has on the cluster is twofold. First, by the way the download queue is implemented in the container runtime, queuing up multiple image download requests prevents legitimate users from deploying workloads that require an image download to be run. Since deleting a container from Kubernetes does not affect the container runtime download queue, this queue can grow uncontrolled
even if the requests are canceled before the download starts
. This starvation can continue for as long as the attacker likes, as long as they have access to the cluster and can request to download fresh images not present on the node.
Secondly, this bug has a significant impact on the target node's resources. This uncontrolled resource usage is untied from any service account or quota and will potentially skew the information available to the scheduler. Furthermore, even a quota of exactly one Pod does not hamper the attack as employing the
--force
flag allows attackers to rapidly deploy downloads and wipe the Pod from the API, never exceeding it.
What did you expect to happen?
As a Pod is deleted but its containers have not been instantiated yet and their image is still being downloaded or is queued for download, such download should be aborted or evicted from the queue as soon as the target node is informed of the deletion.
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Install a fresh Kubernetes cluster using kubeadm. We used versions 1.25 to 1.29. No modifications are needed to any configuration of the cluster. Service Accounts, Quotas, RBAC/ABAC configurations, etc… are not relevant to the attack’s success.
Identify a node to attack in the cluster if there is more than one. Add a NodeSelector to any Pod deployed in subsequent steps so that they can only be deployed on that node.
Identify one or more Docker images that are able to be downloaded from the cluster and are not present in the node’s image cache. The content, configuration, etc.. of the image is irrelevant.
Repeat until there are non-downloaded Docker images available:
Deploy a Pod (with the NodeSelector) of a certain image i;
Wait 1-2 seconds;
Request the Pod’s deletion (possibly with --force)
The victim node’s image download queue will now be filled up with bogus requests, preventing any user's download of further images in the cluster until the attack is stopped and the downloads complete or the node’s containerd process is restarted.
On clusters with k8s version >= 1.27 and MaxParallelImagePulls set to > 1, the attack will still be successful, so long as the attacker manages to request enough images to fill up the parallelism provided by MaxParallelImagePulls.
Anything else we need to know?
We contacted the Kubernetes Security Team in late 2023, and we were informed that this issue is not considered a vulnerability and we could proceed with making it public at our own discretion.
We extensively studied this issue, its impact, limitations and a proof of concept for blocking it in a publication. The paper is currently under evaluation for a submission in a journal, and its preprint is available at this link:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10582
Kubernetes version
This details refer to a specific set of tests we made in the past, but we replicated the attack in several other scenarios.

We assert that a log file on-disk (via CRI-O, or docker's json-file logging driver) should have metadata associated with that log file to describe the UUIDs
and

and
namespace associated with the log output to avoid k8s API calls later.  Today it does not

Line 220

6caf343
return

string

Ideally (and arguably), a log collection system
should not be required
to query the Kube APIs about the log data in order to find the UUIDs of the k8s resource hierarchy associated with a container.  Only
optional
metadata that decorates or enriches the log data would necessitate API calls to fetch that metadata; e.g., if one wanted to decorate logs with one or more labels or annotations from a pod or namespace.  A log collection system should be able to properly disambiguate and group logs accurately without additional API calls which might cause undo burden on the API server.  Since any metadata needed to be fetched via API calls is optional, it can be dropped when inconvenient or added later as a post-processing step.
The "location" of a container in a single k8s cluster is fully described by four pieces of information:
hostname
container UUID (and name)
pod UUID (and name)
namespace UUID (and name)
With the above information, understanding the origin of one or more log entries in an aggregation of logs can be accomplished unambiguously with respect to k8s in one cluster.  Today, it appears that k8s provides 3 of the 4 pieces of data, hostname (implicitly), container, and pod, when constructing the symlink for the log file path.
Can we consider adding namespace UUID and namespace name as well?

[TITLE] Introduce Resource Size as a new Scalability Dimension [BODY] What would you like to be added?
I propose for the introduction of Resource Size as a formal scalability dimension in Kubernetes. The scalability testing is still based on an 8 year old assumption that pods are simple, single-container applications with a minimal resource footprint (tested pods are ~4 KB). However, the evolution of Kubernetes, the rise of machine learning workloads, and the adoption of patterns like init containers and sidecars have led to significantly larger pod objects in real-world scenarios.
This discrepancy creates a significant friction point for users who unexpectedly encounter a hard scalability wall, where a cluster with as few as 50 nodes can become unstable with large pods, despite our official support for 5,000-node clusters.
Recent advancements in the API server (
blogpost
), particularly in caching, response streaming, and API Priority and Fairness (
#132233
), have substantially improved the control plane's ability to handle large resources . We are now in a strong position to formally address this gap, set an official goal for resource size scalability, and provide a more predictable experience for users running complex applications.
Why is this needed?
When Kubernetes scalability goals were developed 7 years ago for the 1.6 release, the assumption was that most workloads would consist of simple, single-container applications. As a result, the size of the pod object itself was not considered a critical factor in scalability testing. Our official scalability tests for 5,000-node clusters still use pod objects of only 4 KB.
However, the Kubernetes ecosystem has evolved dramatically:
Complex Application Architectures: Features like init containers, sidecars, and a growing number of environment variables have "supercharged" pod objects, making them much larger and more complex.
Real-World Usage: We have observed that real-world pod sizes are often significantly larger than our tested scenarios, with pods averaging 10-20KB, and in some cases reaching even 100KB.
A Surprising Scalability Cliff: While Kubernetes supports objects up to 1.5 MB, and our documentation states a 5,000-node scalability target, there is a practical, undocumented limit on pod size that users frequently and unexpectedly encounter. This leads to a poor user experience where they hit a hard scalability wall long before reaching documented limits for other dimensions like node or pod count.
The improvements in K8s 1.34 has shown that the API server can handle much larger resources efficiently. It's time to leverage these improvements to make resource size a first-class citizen in our scalability testing and guarantees.
Proposed Plan
Enable Customization and Baseline Testing:
Add an option to customize resource size in our existing scalability tests.
Introduce a new, non-blocking scalability test with an increased resource size to establish a baseline and understand the current state of performance.
Document and Enforce:
Based on the initial findings, document the current realistic scalability threshold for resource size.
Promote the baseline test to be release-blocking to prevent regressions.
Iterate, Improve, and Decompose:
Begin a cycle of incrementally increasing the resource size in the non-blocking test.
With each increase, identify performance bottlenecks and address them.
As part of this process, develop component-specific benchmarks to isolate and analyze performance, similar to the ongoing work for LIST benchmarks (
#130169
).
Define a Target:
Our proposed initial target is to
target support an average pod size of 100 KB
across our existing 150,000 pod scalability envelope. This goal represents only ~1/15th of the maximum object size supported,  making it resilient for large user application. At that level we expect the resource size will stop being concern for our users at all.
The initial target is soft goal that might be relaxed. The iterative nature of improvements should allow us to stop at any point, whether we encounter a hard blocker or reduction of active contributors.
By making resource size a formal dimension of our scalability envelope, we can provide a much more realistic and reliable experience for the Kubernetes community, ensuring that Kubernetes continues to be the best platform for running all types of workloads, from simple applications to complex, large-scale systems.

/sig api-machinery
/cc

@siyuanfoundation

[TITLE] preStop sleep continues after PID 1 exits [BODY] What happened?
I've configured the podSpec of a Job to include a preStop sleep lifecycle hook. If the Pod is asked to terminate before it completes, the preStop sleep begins and runs for its full duration - even if the Pod completes its processing and PID 1 exits before the preStop sleep is complete. [TITLE] Pod Memory Request=Limit Triggers Pagecache Reclamation and Service Jitter on Node [BODY] What happened?
Description:
When deploying pods on a Kubernetes node with memory request equal to memory limit, despite no memory overcommitment on the host, scheduling a new pod triggers memory reclamation, leading to service jitter for some pods.
Observations:
Monitoring indicates that pagecache reclamation is being triggered.
Before the issue occurs, the node has sufficient memory requests available for scheduling the pod, and the host memory is not overcommitted.
Comparison of RSS (via
ps/top
on the host or
docker stats
) and
container_memory_usage_bytes
(from cAdvisor metrics, which are derived from
/sys/fs/cgroup/<pod_uid>/<container_uid>/memory/memory.usage_in_bytes
) shows a significant difference:
RSS: 14.2GB
container_memory_usage_bytes
: 32GB (equal to the limit)
This discrepancy can be attributed to RSS not including pagecache, while
memory.usage_in_bytes
does.
Questions and Analysis:
If the host memory is not overcommitted and there are sufficient memory requests available for scheduling, why does scheduling a new pod trigger pagecache reclamation?
Given that the limit already constrains the total memory usage (including pagecache), why does this issue arise?

[TITLE] apimachinery scheme initialization matches only on kind [BODY] What happened?
Summary
We have a CRD
experimental.io/v1alpha1/APIGroup
. We're using
kube-state-metrics
to emit metrics for the custom resources, but are receiving the following type mismatch error:
expected type *unstructured.Unstructured, but watch event object had type *v1.APIGroup
The root cause is that dynamic informer uses global scheme to decode objects. If custom resource's
Kind
matches a native kubernetes
Kind
, the scheme returns the native type regardless of the group or the version. The flow is as following:
kube-state-metrics
discovers CRD
experimental.io/v1alpha1/APIGroup
and sets up a dynamic informer that expects type
*unstructured.Unstructured
.
The dynamic informer uses the global scheme to decode objects. During scheme initialization, my custom resource matches a native kubernetes kind
v1.APIGroup
(
https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery@v0.34.0/pkg/apis/meta/v1#APIGroup
).
However, the dynamic informer expects
*unstructured.Unstructured
, causing a type mismatch error.
Detailed Flow
1. Discovery Phase
In
kube-state-metrics/internal/discovery/discovery.go
, it uses a dynamic informer to watch for new CRDs. When a new CRD is added, it parses the CRD spec and stores the discovered GVKs (group, version, kind, plural) in its internal map.
factory := dynamicinformer.NewFilteredDynamicInformer(client, schema.GroupVersionResource{
    Group:    "apiextensions.k8s.io",
    Version:  "v1",
    Resource: "customresourcedefinitions",
}, "", 0, nil, nil)
informer := factory.Informer()
2. Dynamic Client Creation
When
kube-state-metrics
wants to interact with custom resource, it creates a dynamic client. This
resourceClient
is a
dynamic.ResourceInterface
, which is used to list, watch, get, and manipulate resources.
client := dynamic.NewForConfig(config)
resourceClient := client.Resource(schema.GroupVersionResource{
    Group:    "experimental.io",
    Version:  "v1alpha1",
    Resource: "apigroups", // plural
})
3. Listing/Watching Resources
When
kube-state-metrics
wants to list or watch custom resource objects, it calls methods like the following. These methods are implemented in
client-go/dynamic/simple.go
and ultimately make HTTP requests to the Kubernetes API server.
resourceClient.List(ctx, listOptions)
resourceClient.Watch(ctx, watchOptions)
4. Deserialization via Global Scheme
When the API server sends an object (e.g., custom resource),
client-go
’s dynamic client receives the raw JSON. It then calls the global scheme to decode the object.
The scheme tries to find a Go type for the given GVK. If the Kind matches a type registered in the scheme (i.e.,
v1.APIGroup
), even if the group/version are different, it will instantiate that native type.
func (s *Scheme) New(kind schema.GroupVersionKind) (Object, error) {
	if t, exists := s.gvkToType[kind]; exists {
		return reflect.New(t).Interface().(Object), nil
	}

	if t, exists := s.unversionedKinds[kind.Kind]; exists {
		return reflect.New(t).Interface().(Object), nil
	}
	return nil, NewNotRegisteredErrForKind(s.schemeName, kind)
}

func (s *Scheme) Decode(data []byte, gvk *schema.GroupVersionKind, into Object) (Object, *schema.GroupVersionKind, error) {
    // ...
}
5. Type Mismatch Error
The dynamic informer expects all objects to be of type
*unstructured.Unstructured
. But because the scheme found a native type for kind
APIGroup
, it deserializes the object as
*v1.APIGroup
.
When the informer’s event handler runs, it tries to cast the object to
*unstructured.Unstructured
, and hence causing the error:
expected type *unstructured.Unstructured, but watch event object had type *v1.APIGroup
What did you expect to happen?
Scheme initialization should only return a match if the
group
also matches:
func (s *Scheme) New(kind schema.GroupVersionKind) (Object, error) {
	if t, exists := s.gvkToType[kind]; exists {
		return reflect.New(t).Interface().(Object), nil
	}

	// NEW CHANGES
	if t, exists := s.unversionedKinds[kind.Kind]; exists {
		// find a gvk in gvkToType with the same Kind and Group
		for gvk := range s.gvkToType {
			if gvk.Kind == kind.Kind && gvk.Group == kind.Group {
				return reflect.New(t).Interface().(Object), nil
			}
		}
		// if no matching group, do not fallback to Kind-only
	}

	return nil, NewNotRegisteredErrForKind(s.schemeName, kind)
}
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
import (
	"testing"

	metav1 "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime"
	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/schema"

	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"
)

func TestIssue(t *testing.T) {
	nativeGVK := schema.GroupVersionKind{Group: "meta", Version: "v1", Kind: "APIGroup"}
	nativeGV := schema.GroupVersion{Group: "meta", Version: "v1"}
	customGVK := schema.GroupVersionKind{Group: "experimental.io", Version: "v1alpha1", Kind: "APIGroup"}

	// register the native Kubernetes APIGroup type
	scheme := runtime.NewScheme()
	scheme.AddKnownTypeWithName(nativeGVK, &metav1.APIGroup{})
	scheme.AddUnversionedTypes(nativeGV, &metav1.APIGroup{})

	// create a scheme for the custom gvk
	obj, err := scheme.New(customGVK)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	// UNEXPECTED: assert that custom gvk matched native gvk, regardless of group or version
	_, ok := obj.(*metav1.APIGroup)
	require.True(t, ok)
}

behavior:

[TITLE] Pop from the backoff queue whenever the active queue is empty [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Disclaimer: this is a high level description of the idea without providing all necessary details, which can be worked on later whenever there is agreement regarding the general approach.
Whenever the active queue is empty, scheduler could pick the first pod from the backoff queue (the one with the shortest expiration time) and either schedule (assign) it right away or put it back to the unschedulable queue.
The next time the pod goes to the backoff queue it should either use it's previous backoff time if it haven't expired yet, or it should be increased as it is done currently. This way in the worst scenario, pods would have to wait their whole backoff time to get to the active queue (be rescheduled), so not degrade over the current behavior.
Why is this needed?
The main purpose of the backoff queue is to prevent scheduler from processing unschedulable pods over and over again, which can lead to performance degradation of scheduling lower priority pods, including their starvation.
This problem is prominent because rescheduling of unschedulable pods engages time consuming preemption process, which basically depends on the overall number of lower priority pods (see
#128466
).
The higher max backoff time is used, the smaller performance degradation is observed. Unfortunately pods waiting in the backoff queue are "punished" for their unschedulable status by additional waiting time in case when they eventually become schedulable. This form of punishment is a side effect, but not the feature in itself, therefore this change would reduce this punishment time to the very minimum without defeating the purpose of the backoff queue.
With this feature, unschedulable pods could be rescheduled earlier shortening the punshment time to the very minimum, but without impacting scheduler performance. In effect, unschedulable pods would be expected to be rescheduled soon after some event triggered rescheduling (after passing QHints filter).
In the worst case, the backoff queue will work as currently (move pods to active on the backoff time expiration), although having this feature would allow to increase the
maxPodBackoffSeconds
from default 10s to 120s, as in practice the waiting time is expected to be very small anyway. This is important, because there are known reports that 10s backoff time still does not prevent scheduler from running into the starvation problem and the feature in itself won't address it directly, but indirectly by allowing to saftely increase the default time.

[TITLE] TopologySpreadConstraints to specify "max number or % of replicas" [BODY] What would you like to be added?
I didn't find any open or closed issue regarding this topic, so I thought to ask here for feedback.
Today, TopologySpreadConstraints allow us to express distribution conditions focused on how many domains or topologies are created when scheduling a particular workload.
We're managing large multi-tenant clusters and often feel the need to express a "limit" in the topology, such as "I want this workload to be distributed as per maxSkew, but not more than X replicas per node or no more than 10% of the replicas per node."
I'm not an expert in scheduling terminology, but I think adding something like "maxReplicas" (which could be an integer or a percentage) would help with this scenario, expressing the additional conditions mentioned above.
Why is this needed?
In large multi-tenant clusters, where different applications are expected to run on shared nodes, it's useful to specify a further degree of distribution (not more than X replicas per node or not more than Y% per node). This ensures that, in case of node loss, we can control how many replicas per application we can afford to lose. This is particularly important with spot offerings (nodes that can be reclaimed at short notice by the cloud provider).

patchStrategy
for the

field was set to

metav1.

,  and mount
<KUBELET_DIR>/pods/<POD_UID>/<VOLUME_NAME>/mount/subpath
on it.

NotFound

ab3e83f
if
apierrors
.
IsNotFound
(
err
) {

This way, the call to informer's lister would always fail, while the call to client would remain unaffected - this would force the fallback path, ensuring it is present.
What did you expect to happen?
No 404 errors when creating StatefulSets in existing namespaces - even immediately after ns creation.

--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/listers/core/v1/namespace.go

-       errors "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/errors"
        labels "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/labels"
        listers "k8s.io/client-go/listers"
        cache "k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache"
@@ -47,17 +46,3 @@ type namespaceLister struct {

-               // 2. Return not found error if it is

-       }
-       // 3. Otherwise, use the parent implementation from the embedded ResourceIndexer

-}

[TITLE] CVE-2025-9708: Kubernetes C# Client: improper certificate validation in custom CA mode may lead to man-in-the-middle attacks [BODY] CVSS Rating:
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N
—
Medium (6.8)
A vulnerability exists in the Kubernetes C# client where the certificate validation logic accepts properly constructed certificates from any Certificate Authority (CA) without properly verifying the trust chain. This flaw allows a malicious actor to present a forged certificate and potentially intercept or manipulate communication with the Kubernetes API server, leading to possible man-in-the-middle attacks and API impersonation.
Am I vulnerable?
You are vulnerable if:
You use the Kubernetes C# client to connect to a Kubernetes API server over TLS/HTTPS  with custom CA certificates in your kubeconfig file and your connection occurs over an untrusted network.
Affected Versions
All versions of the Kubernetes C# client prior to the next release <=17.0.13
How do I mitigate this vulnerability?
This issue can be mitigated by:
Deploy the patch version of the Kubernetes C# client as soon as possible.
Moving the CA certificates into the system trust store instead of specifying them in the kubeconfig file. Note: This approach may introduce new risks, as all processes on the system will begin to trust certificates signed by that CA. If you must use an affected version, you can disable custom CA and add the CA to the machine's trusted root.
Fixed Versions
Kubernetes C# client >= v17.0.14
Detection
To determine if your applications are affected:
Review your usage of the Kubernetes C# client and inspect certificate validation logic.
Review your kubeconfig files and determine if you use a custom CA certificate (the certificate-authority field in the clusters section).
Review client logs for unexpected or untrusted certificate connections.

A static PV and PVC with bidirectional references (volumeName on PVC and claimRef on PV), or
A static PV and PVC with unidirectional reference (volumeName on PVC only)

[TITLE] Clarify mapping between DRA device classes and extended resources [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Kubernetes has alpha support for requesting a device allocation using the
extended resource
syntax.
What happens if a user puts
deviceclass.resource.kubernetes.io/widget: 42
and
widget-vendor.example.com/iWidget: 1
both in the
.spec
of one particular Pod, when these both equate to the same DeviceClass?
the two requests could be for the same container
or for two different requests, eg a sidecar and the main app container
Proposal: that, contrary to behavior at time of writing, Kubernetes accepts both ways to name the device and sums the requests just as if they all used the same form.
/wg device-management
(previously discussed with the WG via Slack)
Why is this needed?
We can't control what cluster admins do (and mostly we don't want to).
The current approach is that
extendedResourceName
overrides
deviceclass.resource.kubernetes.io/*
.
It has an action at a distance effect; if you as a cluster admin specify
extendedResourceName
for a DeviceClass (maybe you do plan to inject init containers or sidecars), then you shouldn't need to check every Pod template and CI pipeline to know if doing that breaks some existing workload.

[TITLE] Service Multi-Protocol Port Configuration Test Report [BODY] What happened?
Background
Starting from Kubernetes 1.24, Service support multiple ports with different protocols, with this feature becoming stable in version 1.26. This report examines the constraints and behaviors when configuring multiple ports with different combinations of port numbers, protocols, and nodePort values.
Related Issue:
Service port duplication and patch exception
Test Methodology
Test Environment: v1.28.3
Creation Tests:
Create NodePort Services with various port configurations to observe creation success and effectiveness
Patch Tests:
Modify existing Services to test patch behavior and port functionality
Key Findings
Service Creation Behavior
✅
Allowed:
Different protocols with different ports and nodePorts
✅
Allowed:
Same protocol with different ports and different nodePorts
✅
Allowed:
Different protocols with same port but different nodePorts
❌
Blocked:
Same protocol with same port (port conflict)
❌
Blocked:
Same protocol with same nodePort (nodePort conflict)
❌
Blocked:
Any configuration with port conflicts regardless of protocol
Patch Operation Behavior
Patch operations exhibit more complex behavior:
Normal cases:
Same as creation rules for basic scenarios
Anomaly:
When protocols differ but ports/nodePorts conflict, patch commands execute successfully but only the first port item becomes effective
Special Cases
Auto-assigned nodePorts:
When protocols differ and ports are the same without specifying nodePorts, Kubernetes assigns the same nodePort value, causing patch anomalies on subsequent operations
Recovery mechanism:
A second patch operation typically resolves the issue by assigning different nodePort values
Conclusions
Port Configuration Constraints
Same Protocol:
Both port and nodePort must be unique across all entries
Different Protocols:
Recommend ensuring both port and nodePort uniqueness to avoid patch anomalies
Recommendations
Always specify unique port and nodePort combinations regardless of protocol differences
Be aware of patch behavior anomalies when dealing with protocol-mixed configurations
What did you expect to happen?
Ideal scenario is:
(1) When the protocol types are different, the same PORT number should allow the use of the same nodePort, and this state should be achievable through both creation and PATCH.

[TITLE] allowPrivilegeEscalation:false insufficient for privilege escalation prevention [BODY] The issue relates to how allowPrivilegeEscalation: false doesn't prevent all forms of privilege escalation through dangerous capabilities.
When a container's security context sets allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, the current validation only blocks CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability. However, other dangerous capabilities that can also lead to privilege escalation are still allowed.
Technical Details:
Current Validation:
Blocks: CAP_SYS_ADMIN when allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
Allows: CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_MODULE, CAP_SYS_PTRACE, etc.
Example:
apiVersion
:
v1
kind
:
Pod
spec
:
containers
:
  -
name
:
busybox
image
:
busybox
securityContext
:
allowPrivilegeEscalation
:
false
capabilities
:
add
:
["CAP_NET_ADMIN", "CAP_SYS_MODULE"]
#
This is allowed but can lead to privilege escalation
Dangerous Capabilities Still Allowed:
CAP_NET_ADMIN: Network stack manipulation, potential for network namespace escape
CAP_SYS_MODULE: Loading kernel modules
CAP_SYS_PTRACE: Process debugging and memory access
CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH: Bypass file permission checks
CAP_SYS_RAWIO: Direct I/O access
CAP_AUDIT_CONTROL: Audit system manipulation
Impact:
False sense of security when using allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
Privilege escalation still possible through allowed capabilities
Proposed Fix:
Extend the validation to block all dangerous capabilities when allowPrivilegeEscalation is set to false.
I’d love to hear your thoughts! Have you run into situations where
allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
didn’t cut it?
Thanks

[TITLE] Preemption process does not leave a trait in the scheduler cache causing a race [BODY] What happened?
The preemption process that is initiated by the scheduler does not leave the immediate trait in the cache. Due to a race, a pod may come back to the scheduling queue before the in-memory state gets updated (receives a notification about a pod being deleted or marked for deletion DeletionTimestamp != nil) and start the same preemption process again.
Whenever the preemption process identifies a pod eligible for preemption, but learns the pod does no longer exist, it immediately puts the preemptor back to scheduling queue (since it may never receive a notification that wakes it up from the unschedulable queue) and the process repeats in a tight loop, each time producing a pod delete api call.
The factor that triggers this issue is the fact that when a pod being preempted is in the binding process, the scheduler lets it finish the process and IGNORES pod delete notifications, waiting for this async binding process to fail. This creates quite a wide window making the problem very likely to happen in a specific use case, like autoscaling when initial pods jump into nodes they were not intended to and need to be preempted right after). Large number of outgoing api-calls (to delete non-existing pod) generates a big load on the api-server and may generate a snowball effect.
The issue itself exists from a long time, but the PR which closed the loop by activating preemptor pod on failure was added to 1.34
#133213
What did you expect to happen?
The information about a non-existing pod should be reflected in the in-memory cache to cut that loop.
It could be either recorded right after pod delete was accepted or even better whenever any attempt to delete it failed (non-existing pod)
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
We haven't managed to reproduce it in isolation

[TITLE] kubelet: Device plugin fails to connect to new instance of plugin if previous one is terminated [BODY] What happened?
The kubelet fails to connect to the device plugin if a previously running device plugin was running on the node with the same resource name.
Kubelets can get into a situation of running two pods advertising the same device plugin for a brief short period of time. For example, consider the following situation of a vendor hypothetically "upgrading" the device plugin:
kubelet runs
first-device-plugin
advertising resource
example.com/resource
device vendor upgrades device-plugin to
second-plugin
and user deploys it
kubelet switches to use
second-device-plugin
advertising resource
example.com/resource
user deletes
first-device-plugin
Prior to v1.25.0, kubelet would handle this situation, and on step 4, disconnect of
first-device-plugin
would ensure that
first-device-plugin
would be disconnected, and maintain connection to
second-device-plugin
(since it was most recently connected).
This regressed as part of
#109016
where as part of the deletion of the
first-device-plugin
(step 4), kubelet would disconnect from "the most recently" connected plugin, namely
second-device-plugin
, and thus would get into a situation where neither the first or second device plugin would be connected. This would result in kubelet failing to adverting resources for the device. This is because of a bug where kubelet only stores the state of the most recently connected plugin and on disconnect, disconnects the most recently connected plugin.
What did you expect to happen?
I expected kubelet to either maintain the same behavior as pre 1.25: when deleting a device plugin pod, to disconnect from the device plugin that was deleted rather then the most recently connected plugin.
I expect that when a new device plugin connects and the device manager registers it, if an existing device plugin is already running kubelet should handle this situation by either rejecting the registration request or disconnecting from the existing device plugin and connecting to the new one.

CPU/Memory like bandwidth in ResourceQuota/LimitRange
Improve k8s to handle ingress-bandwidth and egress-bandwidth with ResourceQuota and LimitRange
Allow to set bandwidth settings in ResourceQuota as follows.
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
name: pod-and-network-quota
namespace: foo-ns
spec:
hard:
pods: 4
ingress-bandwidth: "1G"  <===
egress-bandwidth: "1G"   <===
Allow to set bandwidth settings in LimitRange as follows.
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
name: cpu-and-network-limitrange
spec:
limits:
type: "Pod"
default:
cpu: 500m
ingress-bandwidth: "10M"  <===
egress-bandwidth: "10M"   <===
defaultRequest:
cpu: 500m
max: # max and min define the limit range
cpu: "1"
ingress-bandwidth: "100M"  <===
egress-bandwidth: "100M"   <===
min:
cpu: 100m
ingress-bandwidth: "1M"    <===
egress-bandwidth: "1M"     <===
Expected behaviors
Reject pod creation when (*):
    ResourceQuota has ingress/egress-bandwidth parmaeters.
    User hadn't set kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth and kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth to their pod.
    LimitRange has no default values for ingress/egress-bandwidth.
Set default value to kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth and kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth of a pod when:
    LimitRange has some default values for ingress/egress-bandwidth.
Reject pod creation when:
    The value of kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth or kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth of a pod is larger/lower than the max/min value of LimitRange.
Reject pod creation when:
    The total kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth values of pods running on the namespace exceeds the ResourceQuota's value.
(*) It's best to reject to pod creation request when pod has no bandwidth annoatation even though ResourceQuota has bandwidth setting, since pod which has no bandwidth annotation can exceeds the quota.
Feature to allow admin to set bandwith limit per port in a container.
Pod level bandwidth limit should be supported by ResourceQuota and LimitRange

Users can set kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth and kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth to their pods.

[TITLE] Convert Go field and type names in autogenerated API docs [BODY] We autogenerate user-facing API documentation from types.go comments now. Most people tend to refer to Go field and type names in their comments as per typical godoc style. However, this isn't appropriate for user docs. I generally tell people to use the json field names instead of Go field names and English instead of type names, but it's been an uphill battle to enforce.
When generating documentation in WriteSwaggerDocFunc, we should try to automatically convert Go field and type names in the comments to json field names and English rather than type names. ParseDocumentationFrom keeps the json field names but discards the Go field names. In general, they should be the same except for capitalization of the first letter, but we could also just keep both in KubeTypes, and replace all occurrences of the Go field name with the json field name in the Doc string. For the type names, we could replace all occurrences of the Go type name with the type name split into separate words at capital letters. For example,
ReplicaSetSpec
would become
Replica Set Spec
. That's not ideal, but
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler List
would be better than
HorizontalPodAutoscalerList
.

[TITLE] Default settings for EvictionHard do not include imagesfs.inodesFree. [BODY] It is possible to deploy Kubernetes with a separate filesystem.  We default the settings for EvictionHard
here
.
A concern is that if users are using the default settings and separate filesystem for images, we are effectively turning off monitoring for INodes on the imagefs.  This means that we won't have disk pressure if inodes run out on the ImageFs.
The fix can be to add
var DefaultEvictionHard = map[string]string{
	"memory.available":  "100Mi",
	"nodefs.available":  "10%",
	"nodefs.inodesFree": "5%",
	"imagefs.available": "15%",
        "imagefs.inodesFree": "5%",
}
To default settings.
This doesn't seem to be a regression as these defaults were added 5 years ago (k8s 1.12) but this could be a potential bug if either users mount a separate filesystem to their container runtime storage or they configure their runtime to store their images on a separate filesystem.

[TITLE] [Proposal] Run once daemonSet (daemonJob) support in Kubernetes [BODY] What would you like to be added?
I: Motivation:
We have some per-node setup works in our platform when provisioning new nodes, but they should operate as an one-shoot manner, so we tried:
daemonSet
, but pods will not run-to-complete, this is not fully what we want. But yes, it can work like idling in a sleep-loop when initialization works finished
batchv1.Job
, we achieved this goal by setting job's
parallelism
(equal to the nodes total number) and injecting
podAntiAffinity
to avoid replicas being allocated in the same node. But when scaling up, we have to re-apply the job and also exclude the former nodes.
We seek the solutions from the community, and found this is widely required, see, maybe more:
Run job on each node once to help with setup
#64623
[DaemonSet] Considering run-once DaemonSet (Job DaemonSet)
#50689
Run-once daemonset
#69001
II: Alternatives:
We also find other ways the community is struggling with:
daemonSet with initContainer, normal container will run with a pause pod to keep alive.
automation suite like Ansible.
Weird ways like making pods unschedulable after running once, see
https://www.sl.id.au/posts/kubernetes-run-pod-once-per-node/
Implement the controller self, like
https://openkruise.io/docs/user-manuals/broadcastjob/
, but this will absolutely lead to the wheel of reimplements in the community.
leverage static pods
III: Proposal
OPT-1. Add a new Job API named like daemonJob(mostly like the daemonSet, but will maintain some features as batchv1.Job), just like deployment vs daemonSet. It behaves as:
ensures that all or a sub-set of Nodes run a copy of a run-to-complete Pod
as nodes are added to the cluster, Pods are added to them
as nodes are removed from the cluster, those Pods are garbage collected
deleting a DaemonJob will clean up the Pods it created.
OPT-2. Add a
runOnce
policy to daemonSet, when pod completes, it will not restart anyway. But I think daemonSet is designed for long-running workloads, so prefer not.
IV: Other requirements related:
CronJob daemonset (previously ScheduledJob)
#36601
Why is this needed?
Met the setup/cleanup demands of run-once pod in all nodes
prevent reimplementing the wheel
🌟 Google doc:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QnAre0Eh8yaDxAnm_3ZrOhbE3d0J-BuieLa25_jzMOE/edit#heading=h.xgjl2srtytjt

[TITLE] Kube-proxy(IPVS): forced resync period changed from 30s to 1h in 1.34 [BODY] What happened?
We observed an IPVS cleanup failure in Kubernetes v1.34.0.
It appears that kube-proxy no longer removes stale IPVS entries outside excludeCIDRs during syncPeriod runs.
What did you expect to happen?
IPVS entries within excludeCIDRs (e.g., 3.3.3.0/24) should remain intact.
IPVS entries outside excludeCIDRs (e.g., 8.5.2.2:80) should be deleted during the next syncPeriod (~30s).
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Configure kube-proxy with:
ipvs:
excludeCIDRs:
- 3.3.3.0/24
syncPeriod: 30s
Manually add IPVS virtual servers:
sudo ipvsadm -A -t 3.3.3.1:80 -s rr   # within excludeCIDRs
sudo ipvsadm -A -t 8.5.2.2:80 -s rr   # outside excludeCIDRs
Verify entries:
sudo ipvsadm -l -n | grep -e 3.3.3.1 -e 8.5.2.2
TCP  3.3.3.1:80 rr
TCP  8.5.2.2:80 rr
Re-check after >10 minutes:
Wed Sep 10 09:21:41 AM UTC 2025
TCP  3.3.3.1:80 rr
TCP  8.5.2.2:80 rr
Wed Sep 10 09:34:53 AM UTC 2025
TCP  3.3.3.1:80 rr
TCP  8.5.2.2:80 rr
Note that both entries persist indefinitely.
Restart the kube-proxy pod → only then the invalid entry (8.5.2.2:80) is removed.
Anything else we need to know?
This issue leads to stale IPVS virtual server entries remaining in the system.
Packets may be forwarded to deleted or invalid backend pod IPs, causing traffic drops and service disruption.

[TITLE] Pod GC should sort by finish Timestamp [BODY] What would you like to be added?
In Controller Manager, terminated pods gc should sort by it's finish time, other than it's creation time.
Why is this needed?
When terminated pods reach gc's threshold (
--terminated-pod-gc-threshold
in Controller Manager, default 12500), Controller Manager will trigger pod gc, delete terminated pods util the pods count below threshold.
But when KCM start deletion, pod sort by creation time, which means pods that created firts will delete first. In some case, like in cluster there are both AI training job and spark job,  spark job running and finish very quick, but some AI pods will running for a long time.
If cluster's total terminated reach gc threshold,  just when long run pods running successfully, it may be gc immediately, because of it's creation time is longest, other workflow controller could not processed it in time.

[TITLE] Change default HPA downscale policy from 100% pods to 25% pods [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Change the
default HPA downscale policy
from allowing 100% pods to be removed in a single step to allowing a smaller percentage (maybe 25%?). This will result in annealed downscaling.
Why is this needed?
The current default downscale policy means that after the stabilization window has passed the downscale recommendation is applied in a single step, regardless of how severe it is. HPA can downscale e.g. from 500 replicas to 1 in a single go.
Such rapid downscaling comes with risks:
a) It's a rapid increase of per-instance load that may have impact on application performance.
b) Potential incorrect (too low) recommendation gets actuated directly. Scaling down step by step (annealed) means calculating a new recommendation in each step, based on new input data, which may fix the bug symptom. It also gives a bit more time for human response.
OTOH rapid downscale is beneficial for some workloads, e.g. batch processing, queue processing. There is a trade-off between cost efficiency and reliability and IMO we should favor reliability by default. Users can override the default to favor efficiency if their use case requires it.

[TITLE] Revisit response compression in k8s API [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Based on load tests and production data gathered from thousands of production k8s clusters, we have observed that gzip compression in k8s API isn't optimal today. Here's the
full doc with details
and the
SIG meeting recording
where this was discussed.
The consensus is this (please add/correct anything I'm missing):
[short-term] Reduce the default gzip level from 4 to 1 in kube-apiserver
[medium-term] Add
DisableCompression
field to kube-config, for clients to disable compression altogether from their end (and avoid
building their own workarounds
)
[medium-term] Add
--disable-compression
flag to kubectl for CLI users to easily turn off compression
[long-term] Make apiserver choose gzip compression level for requests dynamically based on heuristics like object-types and compression ratios achieved (
@smarterclayton
suggested this idea in the past too and we now have data to show its value specifically wrt secrets/configmaps)
[long-term] Explore support for other compression implementations that are faster / less CPU-intensive. Some options are:
zstd -
https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/klauspost/compress/zstd
pgzip -
https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/klauspost/pgzip
snappy -
https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/golang/snappy
CGO-based zlib -
https://github.com/4kills/go-zlib
(pointed by
@simonis
)
I'll own 1, 2 and 3 above. The rest need further eval - probably a KEP.
Why is this needed?
To improve API call latencies (specifically list calls) as well as CPU/memory usage on the apiserver and client side, by trading off for slightly higher network bandwidth usage. The doc linked above has more details.
/sig api-machinery
/sig scalability

[TITLE] Expose cipher suite settings in client-go [BODY] What would you like to be added?
The current client-go
TLSConfiguration
does not expose the underlying net/http
Config
's CipherSuites parameter.
This would allow further exposure of this configuration through controller-runtime and other kubernetes clients to application administrators.
Why is this needed?
As part of delivering FIPS compliant systems, allowing configurability of used cipher suites on both the server and the client side are common requirements.

[TITLE] kube-proxy should report events when the proxier failovers [BODY] What would you like to be added?
kube-proxy should report k8s events of critical cases instead of just logging, e.g., kube-proxy failovers to iptables proxier when it should be running ipvs proxier, see
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.24.3/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_others.go#L588
There might be other critical cases need sysadmin's attention, maybe we should check everywhere.
Why is this needed?
The background is: we recently had kube-proxy’s ipvs scheduling algorithm changed, but one of the nodes didn’t have the corresponding kernel module. When the kube-proxy agent restarts, it failed to enable ipvs proxier, and failovered to iptables proxier. As a result, the ipvs rules and iptables rules are mixed together, causing network issues. I think this kind of failover is rather important, should be reported as k8s events.

[TITLE] Tune APF list work estimator for large responses [BODY] What would you like to be added?
The API Priority and Fairness (APF) mechanism effectively protects the Kubernetes API server from CPU-bound overloads. However, it currently falls short in preventing memory exhaustion, particularly from large LIST responses. The size of LIST responses can vary drastically, ranging from a few kilobytes to hundreds of megabytes. APF's current cost estimation for requests does not adequately account for the memory footprint of these responses. This oversight can lead to API server memory exhaustion (OOMs), reduced stability, and inefficient resource utilization.
Goals
Reduce the maximum memory usage of API server without impact on throughput.
Non-Goals
Model non linear relations in memory usage, this should be reserved for future where we might use a proper model.
Load shedding that happens when cost of upcoming request eshauses CPU causing GC to starve and leak memory.
Proposal
To mitigate memory overloads and prevent OOMs, I propose to incorporate the object size as a primary signal into the APF LIST work estimator. This will allow APF to better reflect the memory cost of these requests and allocate "seats" proportionally, as based on experiments in most cases it is a linear relation.
Specifically, I propose the following changes to the LIST work estimator:
Replace the existing object count estimator with a size-based model:
Requests served from etcd: Assign 1 seat per 100 KB of objects response size.
Requests served from cache: Assign 1 seat per 100 KB of objects response size, however limit it to 1MB. Over that value the cost becomes non-linear which we not model for now.
Increase the global maximum seats from the current 10 to 100. We need bigger range of request cost to properly weight bigger requests.
EDIT: Removed idea to account borrowing into maxSeats estimate based on results in
#132233 (comment)
Above changes could be done one by one, to verify impact of the change on the project.
Why 100KB?
The choice of 100KB per seat is an arbitrary tuning parameter, similar to the current guess of 1 seat per 100 objects. The proposed 100KB value is based on the following observations:
Granularity and Object Size: The maximum object size is 1MB, so a value larger than that would not be effective. A smaller value like 100KB allows the system to better distinguish the cost of single object operations, such as a 100KB put versus a 1MB put.
Memory Variance: We observe a large variance in memory usage for responses of 100KB and 1MB. For 100KB requests, the memory variance is about 2x (between 0.5GB and 1GB), which is within acceptable user expectations. For 1MB requests, memory usage can grow by almost 7x (to 3.2GB), which is not a safety buffer we can reasonably ask users to accommodate.
Experiments
The aforementioned proposal is informed by experiments in which the following behavioral observations were made regarding memory usage when serving LIST requests:
APF nicely scales max QPS to type of request as in most cases thanks to feedback loop that happens during overload. When API server becomes overloaded, the request duration increases reducing number of requests allowed through APF. This works a certain point where cost of accepting requests starts starving GC, however this is realm of load shedding that is outside the scope of this proposal.
There is no linear relation between memory cost of request and number of objects. Rather it increases the CPU cost of allocations and garbage collection, which can indirectly influence memory used. In most cases this is compensated by APF ability to scale to CPU.
In most cases Memory consumption is directly proportional to the object size:
For etcd this relation holds on hide range due to memory mostly coming from needing to load etcd response into memory.
For serving from cache it holds if streaming is disabled. When we enable streaming it this holds well up to 1MB responses, after which it becomes non-linear. This comes from fact that memory comes from encoding and compressing response.
Setup
Experiments were conducted on a Kind cluster with an API server configured with 16 cores and a maximum of 800 concurrent requests. This value was selected because at 800 concurrent requests, the global-default priority level reaches its maxSeats limit of 10. At that value global-default requests are able to borrow up to 500 seats. The cluster utilized the latest Kubernetes build from the master branch, incorporating a patch that allowed the explicit setting of request seats to values of 1, 10, or 100 (bypassing the maxSeats configuration for experimental control).
Metod
For each combination of input parameters (response size, object count, and etcd/cache serving), the following procedure was executed:
Initialize the number of allocated seats to 1.
Determine the maximum Queries Per Second (QPS) that the API server could sustainably serve without hitting any "Too many requests" responses. Run for at 80 seconds to ensure that it's longer than request timeout (default 60s)
At the determined maximum QPS, measure the API server's peak memory usage for different enforced seat values: 1, 10, and 100.

[TITLE] [KEP-4680] DRA: Make device health check timeout configurable [BODY] What would you like to be added?
The timeout for marking a DRA device's health as "Unknown" is currently hardcoded to 30 seconds. This should be made configurable.
This is an update/enhancement for the new DRA Device Health feature being introduced by KEP-4680.
Why is this needed?
As discussed in the review for PR
#130606
(
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130606/files#r2221829511
), a single hardcoded timeout is not ideal for all types of hardware. Different devices (e.g., GPUs, FPGAs, TPUs, storage) may have very different health-reporting characteristics and require different timeout values.
The most robust long-term solution would be to make this a per-plugin setting, allowing each vendor to specify an appropriate timeout for their hardware. This issue tracks the work to add this configurability, which should be a prerequisite for graduating the feature to Beta.

[TITLE] poststarthook/apiservice-registration-controller check blocks apiserver readiness for 1 minute if discovery cannot be completed [BODY] What happened? I’m seeing some odd behavior with 1.28.2 that was not present in earlier releases, with regards to aggregated api services. It appears that the poststarthook/apiservice-registration-controller is now blocking the apiserver from becoming ready for 1 minute, if discovery for an aggregated apiservice is not available when the apiserver is started. Note that this only happens if the apiservice is marked available when the apiserver is started; if it is unavailable at startup (Available status: false), or the service has no endpoints, the health check does not block and readyz returns ok without delay. I am seeing this behavior in 1.28.1 and 1.28.2, but not v1.27.6 or v1.27.5 What did you expect to happen? apiserver becomes ready without any additional delays How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Deploy metrics-server to a Kubernetes cluster Wait for api registration for v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io to complete (Available status is true ). Kill the kubelet and pods on the node hosting the metrics-server pod, such that the metrics-server service continues to show available endpoints, but the endpoint is not reachable. Restart the apiserver before the v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io apiservice is marked unavailable Note that the poststarthook/apiservice-registration-controller check blocks readiness for 1 minute. After 1 minute the Available status is updated to false , and the health check passes. Anything else we need to know? Other notes: Does not appear to make any difference if AggregatedDiscoveryEndpoint feature-gate is set to false. If the metrics-server service has no endpoints available, the apiservice status reason is updated to MisssingEndpoints and the check passes quickly. If there is an available endpoint, but it is not reachable, the check seems to be stuck retrying the endpoint, with the following message repeated in the logs: Sep 18 20:37:01 systemd-node-1 k3s[8000]: E0918 20:37:01.403911 8000 available_controller.go:460] v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io failed with: failing or missing response from https://10.42.0.2:10250/apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1: Get "https://10.42.0.2:10250/apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1": net/http: request canceled while waiting for connection (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers) Odd error from GC that I don't remember seeing in the past: Sep 18 20:34:30 systemd-node-1 k3s[7903]: I0918 20:34:30.744555 7903 garbagecollector.go:816] "failed to discover some groups" groups="" Kubernetes version systemd-node-1:/ # kubectl version Client Version: v1.28.2+k3s-416d7e87 Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3 Server Version: v1.28.2+k3s-416d7e87 Cloud provider k3s OS version systemd-node-1:/ # uname -a Linux systemd-node-1 5.19.0-1019-aws #20-Ubuntu SMP Mon Jan 23 13:41:19 UTC 2023 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux systemd-node-1:/ # cat /etc/os-release NAME="openSUSE Leap" VERSION="15.4" ID="opensuse-leap" ID_LIKE="suse opensuse" VERSION_ID="15.4" PRETTY_NAME="openSUSE Leap 15.4" ANSI_COLOR="0;32" CPE_NAME="cpe:/o:opensuse:leap:15.4" BUG_REPORT_URL="https://bugs.opensuse.org" HOME_URL="https://www.opensuse.org/" DOCUMENTATION_URL="https://en.opensuse.org/Portal:Leap" LOGO="distributor-logo-Leap" Install tools k3s Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable) containerd Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable) flannel

I have Exec Type Liveness and Readiness probes configured as follows.

      exec:
        command:
        - sh
        - -c 
        - 'sleep 8 && echo "liveness"'
      failureThreshold: 3
      initialDelaySeconds: 10
      periodSeconds: 10
      successThreshold: 1
      timeoutSeconds: 10
    readinessProbe:
      exec:
        command:
        - sh
        - -c 
        - 'sleep 8 && echo "readiness"'
      failureThreshold: 3
      initialDelaySeconds: 10
      periodSeconds: 10
      successThreshold: 1
      timeoutSeconds: 10

I could not find any documentation of this change

[TITLE] Proposal for reorganizing getting started guides [BODY] Ideally, users would like instructions that were precise, short, and work with all their existing infrastructure.  But there are too many possibilities, and the kubernetes-dev team can't reasonably update and test across all possibilities.  So, we need to simplify somehow.  This is a proposal/start-of-discussion on how to do that.
Assume users fall into three broad categories:
I want as few steps as possible, and I'm flexible on infrastructure as long as it is cheap and easy.
I want to try on my existing infrastructure and I can't easily change certain choices (e.g. must use RHEL).  I'm used to having to adapt new things to my existing infrastructure, so I can follow longer instructions.
Those who want to develop on kubernetes.
For the first category of user, I suggest we have a couple (3 max) "Quick Start Guides" which:
we ensure are always up-to-date, perhaps somehow testing with each release.
are designed to get people to the point of being able to work the
examples/
as quickly as possible.
I propose that the two "Quick Start Guides" are:
GKE:
for people comfortable signing up for something.
leverages existing Google documentation and support
problem of secret distribution and config distribution is solved by Google.
Vagrant + VirtualBox + Fedora:
the existing vagrant getting-started-guide and Vagrantfile.
for people who don't want to signup for anything or pay anything, or can't access Google Cloud for some reason.
vagrant and virtualbox are pretty easy to install, works on win/os2/linux
problem of secret distribution and config distribution is easy because it is on one physical machine.
For the second category of user, we would have two types of things:
config templates
can be updated by kubernetes devs without fear of breaking a getting-started-guide
getting started guides copy and specialize these templates
example: cluster/saltbase/salt/*
example: docs/getting-started-guides/coreos/cloud-configs/*
a range of specific Getting-started-guides
not officially maintained by kubernetes team
tailored to specific cloud provider, OS, config, and networking choices.
example: docs/getting-started-guides/rackspace.md
example: docs/getting-started-guides/fedora/fedora_manual_config.md
each one has its own copy of any config files it uses
owners periodically review any changes to the "config templates" and apply those to their getting-started-guide.
Developers would typically use the GCE getting-started-guide.

[TITLE] CronJobs should wake up after long time of suspend [BODY] What would you like to be added?

[TITLE] store more event in watch cache when apiserver restart to avoid watch request trigger relist [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Due to the existence of the bookmark mechanism, the difference between the resource version that the client carries when rewatching and the resource version that the apiserver gets from the list in etcd when it starts up is not too big.
It would be nice to be able to cache more events in the watch cache instead of starting from the list resource version returned by etcd to start the cache. The result would be that a client rewatch would not trigger a “too old resource version”.
Why is this needed?
In a stable k8s cluster, when the apiserver of a node is restarted, the clients that list-watched the apiserver before will trigger a relist operation when they re-watch it, and the relist will cause a big burden to the apiserver.

[TITLE] CVE-2024-10220: Arbitrary command execution through gitRepo volume [BODY] A security vulnerability was discovered in Kubernetes that could allow a user with the ability to create a pod and associate a gitRepo volume to execute arbitrary commands beyond the container boundary. This vulnerability leverages the hooks folder in the target repository to run arbitrary commands outside of the container's boundary.
Please note that this issue was originally publicly disclosed with a fix in July (
#124531
), and we are retroactively assigning it a CVE to assist in awareness and tracking.
This issue has been rated High (
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N
) (score: 8.1), and assigned
CVE-2024-10220
.
Am I vulnerable?
This CVE affects Kubernetes clusters where pods use the in-tree gitRepo volume to clone a repository to a subdirectory. If the Kubernetes cluster is running one of the affected versions listed below, then it is vulnerable to this issue.
Affected Versions
kubelet v1.30.0 to v1.30.2
kubelet v1.29.0 to v1.29.6
kubelet <= v1.28.11
How do I mitigate this vulnerability?
To mitigate this vulnerability, you must upgrade your Kubernetes cluster to one of the fixed versions listed below.
Additionally, since the gitRepo volume has been deprecated, the recommended solution is to perform the Git clone operation using an init container and then mount the directory into the Pod's container. An example of this approach is provided
here
.
Fixed Versions
kubelet master/v1.31.0  - fixed by
gitRepo volume: directory must be max 1 level deep
#124531
kubelet v1.30.3  - fixed by
Automated cherry pick of #124531: gitRepo volume: directory must be max 1 level deep
#125988
kubelet v1.29.7 - fixed by
Automated cherry pick of #124531: gitRepo volume: directory must be max 1 level deep
#125989
kubelet v1.28.12 - fixed by
Automated cherry pick of #124531: gitRepo volume: directory must be max 1 level deep
#125990
Detection
To detect whether this vulnerability has been exploited, you can use the following command to list all pods that use the in-tree gitRepo volume and clones to a .git subdirectory.
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.volumes[].gitRepo.directory | endswith("/.git")) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace}
If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact
security@kubernetes.io
Acknowledgements
This vulnerability was reported and mitigated by Imre Rad.

[TITLE] Should provide better information on how to select multiple labels [BODY] Abstractly, what you want to do is this:
pod template in your first replication controller gives the pods it creates the label "version=v1"
pod template in your second replication controller gives the pods it creates the label "version=v2"
your service uses label selector "version=v1 OR version=v2"
However, we don't currently support OR in label queries. Therefore you need to do something like this:
pod template in your first replication controller gives the pods it creates the labels "service=foo" and "version=v1"
pod template in your second replication controller gives the pods it creates the labels "service=foo" and "version=v2"
your service uses label selector "service=foo"

[TITLE] [kubelet] time shift and failed to reserve container name [BODY] What happened? After a liveness failure the kubelet tried to restart the container test-container . The node clock stepped backwards about 40 seconds at the same moment. Because podWorkerLoop calls podCache.GetNewerThan(podUID, lastSyncTime) , the cached pod status never looked newer than the saved lastSyncTime . The kubelet kept the old RestartCount , called CreateContainer again with attempt 1 , and containerd returned: failed to reserve container name "test-container_test-container-68b789996c-q9kxh_d8-cloud-instance-manager_fe9ba7d1-5308-44ef-a81c-83133bf88c50_1": name ... is reserved for "d553f9f992855e898c29b05b6487da56580ab760db155bfd90da20e8fe8a98bc" What did you expect to happen? Even if the node clock jumps backwards, kubelet should notice that the previous container already exists and should wait for a fresh pod status before calling CreateContainer again. The restart attempt should be 2 , not 1 , so containerd does not reject the request How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? Run Kubernetes v1.31.10 with containerd on a test node. Deploy any pod that continuously crashes (e.g. fails liveness probe so it loops in CrashLoopBackOff ). On the same node run: while true do sudo date -s " +10 minutes " sleep 1 sudo date -s " -10 minutes " sleep 1 done Watch kubelet and containerd logs. After several restarts you will see kubelet making a second CreateContainer call with attempt 1 , followed by containerd logging failed to reserve container name . Anything else we need to know? [TITLE] High-throughput container logs cause kubelet log rotation to hang, leading to unbounded 0.log growth (v1.27+ timestamp-based rotation) [BODY] What happened?
What happened:
In Kubernetes clusters running v1.27+, the new timestamp-based container log rotation mechanism (0.log.YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS) fails to rotate logs for high-throughput containers (e.g., >50 MB/s). The 0.log file grows indefinitely (observed >12 GiB), even though containerLogMaxSize is set (e.g., 100Mi).
Kubelet’s log shows repeated "Adding new entry to the queue for processing" every containerLogMonitorInterval seconds, but no "rotateLog" or "rotateLog finished" logs for the affected container — indicating the rotation task never gets executed.

Pasted Graphic.tiff
log config :
containerLogMaxSize: 100Mi
containerLogMaxFiles: 5
containerLogMonitorInterval: 1s
containerLogMaxWorkers: 10
What did you expect to happen?
The kubelet should properly rotate container logs even under high-throughput logging workloads — specifically, the log rotation mechanism should not hang or fail to trigger when a container generates logs at a high rate. The 0.log file should be rotated once it exceeds containerLogMaxSize, preventing unbounded disk usage.

Make all generated applyconfigs implement some common interface that makes them identifiable as such, similiar to
runtime.Object
. How exactly that interface looks doesn't matter, it could be a simple
IsApplyConfig() bool
.
Why is this needed?
In order to be able to offer a good UX for SSA, dynamic clients such as controller-runtimes need a first-class
Apply
or similiar method. In order for that method to be easy to use, it needs to only accept applyconfigs. Because applyconfigs do not implement a common interface, this isn't possible today and such a method needs to accept
any
.

deployments/{name}/rollback
endpoint perform the rollback or 2. have the rollback endpoint simply return a dry-run of the rolled back Deployment which then clients can PUT.

pod-affinity and anti-affinity

This will help the data-intensive workload to achieve fine-grained scheduling to reduce data copying costs.

[TITLE] use AllocatorPool to reduce memory allocation in protobuf stream list [BODY] What would you like to be added? Thanks to @serathius , kube-apiserver now supports the streaming Protobuf list encoder (see PR here ). However, it currently uses the SimpleAllocator as the default memory allocator, which allocates a new byte slice on every encoding operation for every single item in list Objects. Under high-concurrency list request workloads, this results in a significant number of short-lived heap objects, increasing garbage collection (GC) pressure and potentially leading to out-of-memory (OOM) conditions. We propose switching the default memory allocator for Protobuf serialization encoder to runtime.AllocatorPool This change would significantly reduce memory allocation overhead and alleviate GC pressure, especially in streaming list scenarios. Why is this needed? reduce memory allocation overhead and alleviate GC pressure for apiserver

[TITLE] Deployment stuck indefinitely when scaling during rolling update with maxSurge=0 due to stale annotations [BODY] What happened?
When a Deployment is scaled down during an in-progress rolling update (with maxSurge=0),
the deployment controller gets stuck in an infinite loop and the rolling update never completes.
The issue occurs because:
During a rolling update, ReplicaSet annotations (deployment.kubernetes.io/desired-replicas)
are set to the initial deployment size
If the deployment is scaled down while the update is in progress, the replica count changes
but the annotations remain stale
isScalingEvent() detects the annotation mismatch and returns true, causing the controller
to call sync() instead of rolloutRolling()
scale() checks if replica counts match and returns early without updating annotations
(lines 303-304 in pkg/controller/deployment/sync.go)
scaleReplicaSetAndRecordEvent() also has an early return when replicas match (lines 400-401)
The annotations are never updated, creating an infinite loop
This prevents the rolling update from proceeding. Pods remain on the old version indefinitely, and there are no error messages.
Impact:
Applications cannot be updated, security patches cannot be deployed, and the
deployment appears healthy while being completely stuck.
What did you expect to happen?
The deployment controller should update ReplicaSet annotations even when replica counts
already match the desired state. After scaling during a rolling update, the controller should:
Detect the annotation mismatch
Update the stale annotations to match the current deployment.spec.replicas
Continue with the rolling update by calling rolloutRolling()
Create a new ReplicaSet with the updated template
Complete the rolling update successfully
The annotations should be kept in sync with deployment.spec.replicas regardless of whether
the replica count changed, to ensure isScalingEvent() correctly identifies true scaling
events versus stale annotation states.
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

[TITLE] Informer Cache RW Lock Contention Causes DeltaFIFO Backlog and Cache Staleness in KCM. [BODY] What happened?
Summary:
The Kubernetes Controller Manager (KCM) Informer caches experiences read/write mutex contention at scale. KCM controllers frequently acquire a read lock on the Informer cache to list objects from the store, which can starve the CacheController's DeltaFIFO processing from acquiring a write lock to update the Store/Cache during high throughput. This contention can lead to a backlog in DeltaFIFO, delaying delta event processing and stale cache.
Impact
A high backlog in DeltaFIFO results in stale Informer cache data, affecting KCM controllers that rely on it for resource reconciliation. This can lead to incorrect decisions, such as unnecessary resource creation or unnecessary load to APIServer and etcd from KCM Controllers. More details of impact/analysis on Statefulset controller, DaemonSet Controller is provided later in the example section.
Code Flow :
Cache controller
processLoop
pops from DeltaFIFO queue to
processDeltas
.
As cache controller processes deltas, it
adds
or
updates
the store based on
ADD/UPDATE etc events
from DeltFIFO queue.
For Add/Update operations to store,  it acquires lock
here
to update the store.
Meanwhile controller, in the process of
listing pods
, it acquires read lock on store
here
while DeltaFIFO in the above is trying to update the store at the same time.

is also prone to this,  this code path was not exercised in the test.

Impact/Analysis examples :
1. Statefulset Controller
In statefulset controller case, if/when cache is stale and Pod phase status reflects
nil
in cache, even though kubelet has patched the pod to
Running
phase, Statefulset controller will keep trying to
create pods and get 409's  - conflict as it exists in etcd
as this
condition
will evaluate to true
When I patched the KCM Statefulset controller, I can see that just
LISTING
pods from informer cache in statefulset controller when there are lots of pods in single namespace can take upto at peak
~980 ms
, which creates a huge backlog in DeltaFIFO during this time.
In Statefulset controller, in the process of
listing pods
, it acquires read lock on Store
here
while DeltaFIFO in the above is trying to update the Store at the same time ( will cover on this more below)

12 trace.go:236] Trace[410148869]: "DeltaFIFO Pop Process" ID:kube-system/kube-proxy-fv428,Depth:229809,Reason:slow event handlers blocking the queue ... (total time: 321ms):

In DS conttoller it does similar thing ,
listing all pods from cache
holding a read lock,  which blocks all that time from updating the store in Process Deltas.

Ideally Controllers should be isolated from each other to avoid noisy neighbor problem, which isn't possible due to Controllers sharing Shared InformerCache.
Long Term

Food for thought:
Introduce a dedicated Indexer/Cache solely for DeltaFIFO writes and syncing it  in a separate routine  to a separate Indexer/Store for controllers to read from can reduce lock contention from list from downstream controllers.
However, this means controllers will operate on slightly delayed data, which is much better than super stale data at scale, we need to ensure this copy is light weight unlike Huge lists that controllers do today which worsens the contention. This will help APIMachinery code has more control on these components performance instead of depending on implementations of downstream controllers.
Main thing about this theory is that - we need to ensure we are not shifting the problem to second cache to reduce overhead in first cache :)  , we can something similar to what etcd does today, if difference between applies and commits b/w first cache and second cache is like say
X

This comes with a con of increasing the memory overhead  because its essentially storing a separate cache copy.
This requires changing pieces of API Machinery architecture as it stands now.
This approach might not only help KCM controllers but any controllers relying on caches built out of API Machinery code that runs on Dataplane Nodes.
At the minimum in short term

we should ensure all Controllers under KCM avoid heavy list operations on the Informer Cache/Store to reduce lock contention.
Build and utilize Indexers where applicable to minimize the number of items fetched, reducing read lock duration and improving cache update efficiency.

[TITLE] Pod & Container Lifecycle [BODY] Hello,
Problem:
Insufficient information about the pod lifecycle and how a pod's state maps to the pod's containers' states. Specifically the documentation states that "The phase of a Pod is a simple, high-level summary of where the Pod is in its lifecycle. The phase is not intended to be a comprehensive rollup of observations of Container or Pod state, nor is it intended to be a comprehensive state machine"
Pod Lifecycle
Proposed Solution:
Specify the pod lifecycle and how a pod's state maps to the pod's containers' states, exit codes, and liveness probes.
The following statements reflect my understanding of the pod's lifecycle, please do post comments and corrections as appropriate.
Pod Lifecycle
Container Lifecycle
The Kubelet determines a pod's state exclusively based on the pod's
init containers'
state
exit code
main containers'
state
exit code
liveness probe
Pending
When a Pod is in the state Pending then
none of the Pod's Init Containers are in the state Terminated[Failure]
all of the Pod's Main Containers are in the state Waiting
fact {
    all p : Pod | 
        p.status = Pending <=> {
            // Init Container
            no  c : p.init_containers | c.status = Terminated_Failure
            // Main Container
            all c : p.main_containers | c.status = Waiting
        }
}
Running
When a Pod is in the state Running then
all of the Pod's Init Containers are in the state Terminated[Success]
at least one of the Pod's Main Containers is in the state Running
none of the Pod's Main Containers are in the state Terminated[Failure]
none of the Pod's Main Containers are dead
fact {
    all p : Pod | 
        p.status = Running <=> {
            // Init Containers
            all  c : p.init_containers | c.status = Terminated_Success 
            // Main Containers
            some c : p.main_containers | c.status = Running 
            no   c : p.main_containers | c.status = Terminated_Failure
            no   c : p.main_containers | isDead[c]			
        }
}
Success
When a Pod is in the state Success then
all of the Pod's Init Containers are in the state Terminated[Success]
all of the Pod's Main Containers are in the state Terminated[Success]
all of the Pod's Main Containers were live
fact {
    all p : Pod | 
        p.status = Success <=> {
            // Init Containers
            all c : p.init_containers | c.status = Terminated_Success 
            // Main Containers
            all c : p.main_containers | c.status = Terminated_Success 
            all c : p.main_containers | isLive[c]
        }
}
Failure
When a Pod id in the state Failure then
all of the Pods Init Container are in the state Terminated
all of the Pod's Main Containers are in the state Terminated
and
at least one of the Pod's Init Containers is in the in the state Terminated[Failure]
or
at least one of the Pod's Main Containers is in the in the state Terminated[Failure]
or
at least one of the Pod's Main Containers was dead
fact {
    all p : Pod |
        p.status = Failure <=> {
            // Init Containers
            all c : p.init_containers | c.status = Terminated  
            // Main Containers
            all c : p.main_containers | c.status = Terminated
            // Init & Main Container
            (some c : p.init_containers | c.status = Terminated_Failure) or (some c : p.main_containers | c.status = Terminated_Failure) or (some c : p.main_containers | isDead[c]) 
        }
}
Caveats
Note that the
current
state is trailing the
genuine
state, since Kubernetes in general and the Kubelet in special use polling.
current state at t: Pending, genuine state at t: Running
Is this an accurate reflection of Kubernetes' behavior?
