[TITLE] RFE Optional CronJob Parameter: Auto-Suspend Kubernetes CronJob After Specified Number of Successful Executions [BODY] What would you like to be added?
/sig apps
/assign
Want to get feedback on this proposal. I can proceed to KEP process later, if it looks worthy for it to everyone.
Feature Summary
This RFE proposes adding an optional parameter to Kubernetes CronJobs that allows setting a maximum number of successful executions for a job, after which the job automatically is suspended. This feature would help manage resource usage (optionally) and ensure tasks do not run indefinitely and benefit those use cases where you want to check something for few times but not forever, similar to the 'at' command but within a Kubernetes environment.
Context
While Kubernetes supports scheduled jobs via CronJobs, there is currently no native feature to automatically stop these jobs after a certain number of successful completions. This enhancement would allow users to set limits on job executions, which is interesting in some cases.
Technical Details
Implementation could involve extending the
CronJob
specification to include an
.spec.successfulJobCountLimit
optional attribute, which defines the maximum number of successful executions before the crojob suspends. Kubernetes' job controller would need to be enhanced to track the count of successful executions and update the job's active status accordingly.
Example of cronjob using this optional parameter
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: example-cronjob
  namespace: default
spec:
  schedule:
"
0 1 * * *
"
successfulJobHistoryLimit: 3
#
This keeps the last three successful job records
successfulJobCountLimit: 5
#
Hypothetical property to suspend the CronJob after 5 successful executions
jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: hello
            image: busybox
            args:
            - /bin/sh
            - -c
            - date
;
echo
Hello from the Kubernetes cluster
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
Why is this needed?
Consider a scenario where temporary cronjobs are created dynamically and jobs are scheduled for specific operational checks or data processing tasks that only need to run a predetermined number of times. Without a native feature to limit executions, developers must implement additional logic to track and suspend the cronjobs.
This feature is particularly beneficial in scenarios such as:
Jobs that are relevant only for a specific duration or a limited number of executions.
Certain tasks may need to be run a specific number of times to meet regulatory requirements.
Environments where jobs need to run a finite number of times to test and validate software under controlled conditions.
Some notes
Having a finish date/time, instead of force X number of executions is a potential other solution that could work for this use-case.
Practical use case
In my practical use case, my backend needs to monitor if an Instagram story has been removed. Since Instagram stories are ephemeral and last only 24 hours, I need a system that can perform checks several times within that period. The checks are triggered whenever a new story is detected.
I utilize Kubernetes cronjobs to manage these checks, as Kubernetes provides reliable scheduling to ensure the tasks are executed on time. However, the challenge arises with the cleanup of these dynamically generated cronjobs. As new stories can be added at any time, cronjobs can accumulate rapidly, leading to clutter and unnecessary use of resources and inconsistent results if these are not marked to run for few times during the day. Manually cleaning up these cronjobs isn't practical, especially when managing them in large numbers, which could easily exceed 100.
To address this issue systematically and possibly assist others in the community facing similar challenges, I proposed a Request for Enhancement (RFE). This proposal aims to explore solutions for automating the cleanup process of dynamically generated cronjobs in Kubernetes environments.

[TITLE] Cronjobs occasionally run much later than scheduled [BODY] What happened?
CronJobs will occasionally fail to create their Jobs at the scheduled time, with delays ranging from 3 minutes to over 50 minutes. In the most extreme cases we've observed delays over 60 minutes.
From the kube-controller-manager logs, if I'm understanding correctly (which i may not), it appears that CronJobs rely exclusively on the reconciliation process to trigger Job creation. If no reconciliation occurs around the scheduled time, the Job is not created until a subsequent reconciliation cycle is triggered.
Logs consistently show the following pattern (verbosity set to 8), even for CronJobs that execute on time, this job ran 5 minutes later than scheduled:
I1120 11:05:32.562672       1 cronjob_controllerv2.go:526] "No unmet start times" logger="cronjob-controller" cronjob="camel-test/mkt-cloud-segments-servicecloud-v2-simu-buidar-pp"

Performing manual actions, such as editing the CronJob object or deleting an old Job, forces an immediate reconciliation and triggers the creation of the pending Job.
Another thing we observed is that the issue only affects cronjobs that run on a daily basis (these are distributed at different times) but those that run frequently, like every 15 minutes, never get delayed.
Things we checked:
Control-plane clocks verified: All clocks are synchronized using NTP. No drift observed.
Increased logging verbosity: Enabled v=8 for kube-controller-manager
The number of cronjobs does not seem to be too much for the size of the cluster and resource utilization
We don't know what could be causing this behavior and we don't know how to continue debugging it further.

CronJobs should create their corresponding Jobs at the scheduled time.

Connection: close

.

nil
it generates new empty hash, sets some default values, but then does:

.

=
headers
req
.

headers
.
Get
(
"Host"
)

was previously set (I assume by

[TITLE] Improper Permissions on ConfigMap and Secret Mounts [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Hey, I am opening this issue publicly as it was approved by a member of the Kubernetes staff on HackerOne (#2867563) to be discussed with the larger community. Since addressing it would break existing users, it may require a Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal (KEP). The staff member also agreed that it is a poor default.
Description
Kubernetes mounts ConfigMaps and Secrets to containers with default permissions -rw-r--r-- (644) also the permission on the ConfigMaps and Secrets directories mounted to the container is set to -rwxrwxrwx (777),
This configuration allows any user in the container, not just the root user, to read these files, exposing sensitive data and violating the principle of least privilege.
In multi-user containers, any non-root user can access these ConfigMaps and Secrets, further increasing the risk of unauthorized data exposure.
To prevent this, users can use the defaultMode parameter to set stricter permissions, such as 600/750, ensuring only the root user has access.
The current default behavior conflicts with the principle of least privilege, making manual adjustment necessary to protect sensitive data.
Steps To Reproduce:
Create a Kubernetes ConfigMap or Secret.
Mount the ConfigMap or Secret into a container.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secret-mounted-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: my-app
      image: nginx:latest
      securityContext:
        runAsUser: 1000
      volumeMounts:
        - name: secret-volume
          mountPath: "/etc/secret"
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: secret-volume
      secret:
        secretName: my-secret
Run the container with multiple users, including a non-root user (e.g., user ID 1000).
Observe that the default permissions are -rw-r--r-- and that any non-root user can read the mounted data.
Why is this needed?
To mitigate this risk, we need to ensure that the directory and the mounted files of Configmaps/Secrets have permissions set to 750. This setting allows only the root user and the group owner to read and execute, while preventing access by other users.
his approach limits read access to the root/owner only, thereby following the principle of least privilege and reducing unauthorized exposure of sensitive data.

[TITLE] Capability to pull images from other worker nodes in the cluster before pulling from remote registry. [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Add capability to pull a docker image from another worker node that has already downloaded the same docker image before pulling from remote registry.
In addition, when the deployment calls for multiple replicas and the image isn't yet available on any worker node, limit pulling from remote registry to just one worker node then instruct other worker nodes where replicas are running to pull from the worker node that now has the image.
Why is this needed?
When working with large images (
>1GB
) and private docker registry, combined with a slow network and a CRI that has no image pull progress makes for a really bad user experience.  Pulling an image from my private registry to where the k8s cluster is located takes upward of 15 minutes.
Current workaround - using BASH script to pull and distribute docker image to all worker nodes before apply deployment YAML to cluster.

[TITLE] LimitRange and ResourceQuota Accept Values Without Units, Leading to Pod Scheduling and Runtime Failures [BODY] What happened?
When creating a LimitRange or ResourceQuota without specifying units for memory and storage (e.g., "2" instead of "2Gi"), Kubernetes accepts the resource creation. However, pods fail to be scheduled, resulting in the following error:
Error creating: pods "...": [maximum memory usage per Pod is 2, but limit is 1Gi, maximum memory usage per Container is 2, but limit is 1Gi]
Upon adjusting pod resource requests and limits to omit units (e.g., memory: 1), pods schedule but remain stuck in the ContainerCreating phase with containerd errors:
Failed to create pod sandbox: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to create containerd task: failed to create shim task: OCI runtime create failed...
What did you expect to happen?
Kubernetes should reject LimitRange or ResourceQuota configurations without specified units for memory and storage.
Alternatively, Kubernetes should normalize the values to a default unit to ensure compatibility.
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Create a LimitRange without units for memory:
yaml
`apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
name: example-limitrange
namespace: test-namespace
spec:
limits:
type: Pod
max:
memory: "2"
min:
memory: "500m"
type: Container
max:
memory: "2"
min:
memory: "250m"
`
Create a ResourceQuota without units:
apiVersion: v1 kind: ResourceQuota metadata:   name: example-resourcequota   namespace: test-namespace spec:   hard: limits.memory: "4" requests.memory: "4"
Deploy a pod with the following resource configuration:
resources:   requests: cpu: 500m memory: 512Mi   limits: cpu: 500m memory: 1024Mi
5.Observe pod creation failure with FailedCreate event.
6.Update the pod memory to omit units:
resources: requests: cpu: 500m memory: 1 limits: cpu: 500m memory: 1
7. Observe pod stuck in ContainerCreating state with containerd errors.
Anything else we need to know?
This issue occurs consistently across multiple clusters. ( EKs , k3s ...)
Errors in the ContainerCreating phase point to systemd and containerd issues when using unnormalized values

[TITLE] Feature request: reserving memory buffer for workload on a cluster node [BODY] What would you like to be added?
We would like to be able to reserve some amount of memory (
buffer
) for our workload on a cluster node.
Scheduler should not over-subscribe a
New Allocatable
=
Allocatable
-
buffer
.
Node-pressure eviction
should still use an “old”
Allocatable
for evicting pods.
Why is this needed?
This memory buffer would allow us to withstand memory consumption spikes and avoid OOMKilled errors.
This memory buffer would be available for any pod from our workload if this pod happens to temporarily need significantly more memory than configured in a memory request setting.
Such memory buffer would be especially helpful if
Memory QoS
feature gets enabled.
We have very dynamic workload. We run a service which executes customer’s builds. For every new build our service creates a new pod that lives for a short time.
Memory consumption of such a pod can vary. In some cases it can try to consume significantly more memory than configured in a memory request setting of the pod.
If a node is fully packed with pods, it can lead to OOMKilled error and pod eviction.
We can only roughly guess possible memory consumption value because it depends on build type and build configuration provided by a customer.
Therefore, memory request settings which we configure cannot be precise.
Currently, we need to configure quite high memory request setting to minimize a likelihood of OOMKilled errors.
This is very cost inefficient because we waste a lot memory on a node.

[TITLE] DRA drivers: helper code for checking device allocations [BODY] What would you like to be added?
A DRA driver has to check in NodePrepareResources whether the devices are a) already prepared for other claims and b) really currently available.
If so, it has to refuse to prepare them again. This is a sanity check that acts as last line of defense against unintended concurrent usage of a device (case a) or race conditions. DRA tries hard to avoid such situations, but at least the
"device became unhealthy"
is inherently racy. Allocating the same device for different claims could be the result of a bug or allocation by different schedulers without
coordination
.
DRA driver authors might forget to implement this check. Perhaps we can move it into
k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/kubeletplugin
with such an API change that the driver authors are forced to do something?
Why is this needed?
Higher quality of DRA drivers.

[TITLE] Kubernetes OIDC requires authentication for well-known and JWKS endpoints, contrary to OIDC Specification [BODY] What happened?
Kubernetes' OIDC authentication mechanism enforces authentication when querying the OIDC provider’s /.well-known/openid-configuration and JWKS (/keys) endpoints. This behavior contradicts the OIDC specification, which states that these endpoints must be publicly accessible.
The primary issue is that many services supporting resource server authentication (such as RabbitMQ and OpenSearch) rely on OIDC token validation but fail to work with Kubernetes OIDC due to the enforced authentication on these endpoints. These services expect to fetch the discovery and public keys without authentication, as per the OIDC spec, but Kubernetes' behavior prevents this, breaking compatibility with standard OIDC validation flows.
What did you expect to happen?
Kubernetes should allow unauthenticated access to these endpoints, as OIDC-compliant providers may not require authentication for retrieving discovery (/.well-known/openid-configuration) and signing keys (/keys).
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
GET
https://api.k8s,example:6443/.well-known/openid-configuration
E.R. get well-known without authentication

[TITLE] Proposal: Add status.data in Job/CronJob to pass job output [BODY] What would you like to be added? Currently, the status section in Job/CronJob workload contains fields succeeded/active/failed , etc. But usually we need the job to pass the output data, to let us do more logic rely on the result data. So propose to add status.data in Job/CronJob to pass the job output, the data field type could be a string, then it can support more complex json string. Demo: apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: Job ... status: completionTime: "2022-11-04T15:38:37Z" startTime: "2022-11-04T15:37:14Z" succeeded: 1 data: '{"repo":"my-repo","imageTag":"v1.4.4-24.g5e8cc5be"}' // output data Why is this needed? Usually, we run a job A, then run a controller or a script which need the job output data to do more logic. But currently the Job/CronJob status does not support data output, so propose to add status.data to achieve it.

[TITLE] /api/..../service/proxy broken for service not backed by pod [BODY] We have a service with an endpoint that is not for a pod but a process that (for technical reasons not relevant to this report) needs to run outside Kubernetes.
That service works fine, except we also want to be able to access it via the proxy api path.
When we do that, we get the unhelpful error message "no endpoints available for service ".
In our case, this error is false: there is an Endpoint (if there wasn't then the service wouldn't work). There are many reports of this error message causing confusion because, e.g., the port name isn't given or some other reason, but in our case the problem is in
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go
where a function isValidAddress() assumes that every service is backed by a pod.
If it is backed by something else (outside Kubernetes) then the error is output and the proxy mechanism can't work.
@thockin
: "do we really need this check?" No, please remove it!
Kubernetes version 1.19, present in current source code today as linked above.
I should also mention that I did see the restrictions at
https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/#services-without-selectors
and they do not apply, i.e., the endpoint does not point at link-local/loopback/virtual cluster IP.

[TITLE] CEL Validation: Add 'optionalSelf: true' config for consistency with 'optionalOldSelf: true' [BODY] Add 'optionalSelf: true' config for consistency with 'optionalOldSelf: true'
Labels:
/kind feature
/sig api-machinery
why we need it?
This is a feature request to add a new optionalSelf boolean field to the x-kubernetes-validations rule definition.
When set to true, this configuration would change the type of the self variable within the Common Expression Language (CEL) expression to be an "optional". This would mirror the existing optionalOldSelf: true configuration, which does the same for the oldSelf variable.
This addition would provide a consistent and more readable syntax for writing rules that need to check for the presence of fields, especially for rules that must work across both CREATE and UPDATE operations.
Motivation:
A common validation use case is to prevent a field, once set, from being unset. For example, a user may set an optional field like spec.replicas. Future updates should not be allowed to remove this field from the object.
With the current tooling, this rule is written using the
// Prevent spec.replicas from being unset
'!has(oldSelf.replicas) || has(self.replicas)'
This rule correctly implements the logic: "either the old object did not have the field, or the new object must have the field".
This rule needs to define on the parent object, far from the field is defined.
Proposal:
Introduce a new boolean configuration field, optionalSelf, to the validation rule definition. When optionalSelf is set to true, the self variable in the CEL expression will be treated as an optional, gaining the same hasValue() and value() helper methods that oldSelf gets via optionalOldSelf: true.
With this change, the rule above could be present on the field itself.
// The proposed, more readable syntax.
// This would require both
optionalOldSelf: true
and the new
optionalSelf: true
.
oldSelf.hasValue()  == self.hasValue()
Advantages:
Improved Readability and Symmetry: The proposed syntax is cleaner and more self-documenting. The parallel structure of oldSelf.hasValue() and self.hasValue() makes the rule's intent immediately obvious.
Consistency: It provides a single, consistent mechanism for checking field presence on both object states (oldSelf and self), removing the need to mix methods and global functions.
Example Use Case
Consider a CRD where the replicas field is optional but should be immutable in its presence after being set.

[TITLE] Document Kubernetes approach to Go versions in release branches [BODY] What would you like to be added?
I'd like Kubernetes to state the position on updating the Go language version used for release branches.
Why is this needed?
I couldn't find a publicly stated Kubernetes policy around Go version updates for release branches documented anywhere. Right now, Kubernetes maintains releases for a year, but doesn't appear to update the Go version.  Go makes new releases 2x/year and supports only 2 releases. If a Kubernetes version (such as v1.23) stays on the same Go release (as it does with Go 1.17) for the whole release's lifetime, it will enter a period where the version of Go being used is no longer supported with CVE updates. This is presently the case where Go 1.17 received security releases on 2022-08-01 but didn't on 2022-09-06 when go1.18.6 and go1.19.1 were released.

[BODY] xref #116667 which was "resolved" with #116672 xref #73760 xref #40610 We have the "downward API" which extracts almost exclusively information which is represented as fields on "this pod" and projects either env vars or files on disk. But there's a slow but non-zero trickle of requests to extract info from other places (e.g. "this node"). This is less obviously reasonable because it could turn into a confused-deputy, exposing information that the pod is not actually authorized to know. In #73760 (comment) (more than 2 years ago!) I suggested people use a sidecar to get and format the info. We have never actually made such a sidecar image, leaving it as an exercise for the reader. Can / shold we do better? The existing image (registry.k8s.io/kubernetes/kubectl) seems to serve two purposes: as a portable CLI when you don't have kubectl installed as this sidecars It works for #1 , but is not super useful for #2 without some sorts of tools in the image. How would we feel about either pivoting it or adding a new kubectl-sidecar image and adding a bunch of useful shell tools? E.g. bash grep sed awk head tail jq diff coreutils (mv, ln, cat, sleep, ...) In short, I think it should be possible for people to write something like: while true; do kubectl get -o json node $THIS_NODE | jq -r '.status.conditions[] | [.type,.status] | @tsv' | grep Ready | cut -f2 > .ready.tmp mv -f file.tmp ready sleep 10 done cc @dims since you touched the image before :)

[TITLE] [FG:InPlacePodVerticalScaling] Improve allocated resources checkpointing [BODY] There is some low-hanging fruit for improving the checkpointing of allocated resources:
When the pod allocation is updated, the Kubelet always calls set allocation at the pod level, but the status manager sets it for each container, calling through to the checkpoint state. This causes the checkpoint file to be written in quick succession for each container in the pod. It would be better to just update the checkpoint once per-pod.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/status/state/state_checkpoint.go#L138
Failure to write the checkpoint should be logged, but not block the resize from proceeding with the in-memory cache. The checkpoint is only used on kubelet restart, and the failure state for that looks the same whether or not syncing the pod proceeds. Better to treat the checkpointing as best effort.
I changed my mind about this. Better to not mask the problem. If the checkpoint can't be written on resize, better to leave the resize in a deferred state, otherwise we risk the node becoming unstable on restart.

[TITLE] Gracefully transition traffic when change selector of loadbalancer service [BODY] What would you like to be added?
We hope when change selector of Loadbalancer service to transition traffic from one backend to another, the status of pool member in Loadbalancer on cloud provider side can be automatically updated.
I assume the process is like below. 'blue' and 'green' stands for two backend pod labels.
After changing the selector from 'green' to 'blue', Kubernetes would first modify the endpoints to point to both nodes simultaneously. Then, the Kubernetes OpenStack Cloud Provider plugin modifies the load balancer pool status, disabling 'green'. This way, there won't be any new traffic being routed from the load balancer to 'green'. Then, Kubernetes proceeds to modify the endpoints to 'blue', completing the graceful switch from 'green' to 'blue'.
Why is this needed?
Because when I change the selector of a Loadbalancer service I found there is always a break (less than 15sec) to establish a new connection via the loadbalancer ip address. I suppose this issue is caused by the health monitoring from loadbalancer is later than the health check of kube-proxy. So the status of pool member cannot be updated in time. The Loadbalancer still distribute the traffic to the old backend although it has been already unhealthy. So that the break occurs. If changing selector can be graceful this issue would be avoided.

[TITLE] not increment pInfo.Attempts when the scheduling fails with Error status [BODY] The current
pInfo.Attempts
is simple; when the scheduler
Pop()
the pod, it increments
pInfo.Attempts
.
And, also this
pInfo.Attempts
is used to calculate the backoff time.
There are basically two failures that the scheduling cycle could make; Unschedulable or Error.
Unschedulable: the Pod is unschedulable; e.g., no node has enough resource, nodeaffinity, etc.
Error: the Pod cannot be scheduled because of unexpected errors;  e.g., kube-apiserver is unstable, network issue, etc.
Given
the backoff is a penalty of wasting the scheduling cycle
, we shouldn't increment
Attempts
when the Pod comes back to queue with Error status
so that the backoff time doesn't get longer by those errors.
As the actual example, what could happen now is:
The scheduler fails to schedule all the pods because the cluster is under the networking issue.
pInfo.Attempts
in all the Pods gets bigger and bigger meanwhile.
The network issue is resolved and some Pods go scheduled.
But, then if some Pods fail, they have a large
pInfo.Attempts
, and hence gets super long backoff time, which is unfair because the most of their
Attempts
are failed not by the scheduling reason, but by the network issue.
/kind feature
/assign
/sig scheduling

[TITLE] GOAWAY are not handled gracefully in apiserver when aggregating [BODY] What happened?
Hey folks,
After some debugging, I figured our that apiserver is not handling gracefully
GOAWAY
events from downstream services when aggregating.
In our case, under high load we would receive erros like:
Response body: error trying to reach service: http2: Transport: cannot retry err [http2: Transport received Server's graceful shutdown GOAWAY] after Request.Body was written; define Request.GetBody to avoid this error
even if we would be connecting with HTTP/1.1 to the
apiserver
which gave then a hint that the error is downstream.
┌──────────────────┐                       ┌──────────────────┐
┌──────────────────┐                │                  │                       │                  │
│                  ├────────────────▶                 ─┼───────HTTP/2.0────────▶                  │
│   User Request   │                │  kube-apiserver  │                       │  kube-apiserver  │
│                  ◀───503 error────┤  (aggregating)   │                       │    downstream    │
└──────────────────┘                │                ▲◀┼────Sending GOAWAY ────┤                  │

                                                     │                                             
                                           GOAWAY is not retried

As the error indicates to properly handle
GOAWAY
events, so the Go client tackles retrying, without propagating the error directly to the users.

[TITLE] Support takeover for devicemanager/device-plugin [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Add support for seamless takeover by a new device-plugin for a resource without deregistering the resource.
In other words, a new device-plugin can be started and registering the resource before the old device-plugin is stopped. In this case, devicemanager should not change the values of allocatable/total count for this resource.
Why is this needed?
Currently, devicemanager only works with one device-plugin instance for every resource. In other words, if two device-plugin are running, devicemanager may have unexpected behaviors.
For example, when two device-plugin are running, they are both registered for the same resource. However, if one of them stops, the resource is marked as deregistered and resource counts reset to 0.
We need this support to have seamless deployment of device-plugin. After this is supported, new device-plugin can be started while the old device-plugin is also running, and devicemanager should notice the new device-plugin, as it registers more recently, to be the new takeover and gracefully deregister/disconnect the old device-plugin. With this, there will be no downtime for resources in device-plugin updates.

[TITLE] The pod is in the UnexpectedAdmissionError state. [BODY] What happened?
We found that after the kubelet process restarts, some pods dependent on device plugins may enter the UnexpectedAdmissionError state.
The reason is that when the kubelet restarts, it retrieves the pod list from the apiserver and begins processing the pods. At this point, the device plugin has not yet had the chance to register, which can cause the pods to enter an UnexpectedAdmissionError state. As a result, the containers are killed, and the workload then pulls up a new replica.
Assuming the service has only two replicas, the aforementioned reasons may lead to the pod being rebuilt, during which the service will be interrupted.
What did you expect to happen?
Containers should not exit due to kubelet restarts.
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Configure the pod to depend on the device plugin and restart kubelet.

The leader election acquisition loops currently attempts indefinitely to acquire a leader, even if the cluster is unreachable.

We should introduce a configurable timeout to bail out and fail the leader election process if the cluster is not reachable within a specified time. [TITLE] Add Verbose Logging to net/http for Egress Auditing and Rename probe/http/http.go [BODY] What would you like to be added?
This proposal includes two related changes to improve egress traffic visibility from core Kubernetes components and to refine logging controls:
Add Verbose Logging to staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go: Introduce new klog V-level logs to provide visibility into outbound HTTP requests and how they are handled by proxy settings.
A V(5) log will be added to record requests that are proxied (i.e., not matching the NO_PROXY environment variable). This helps identify traffic that would be blocked in a restricted environment.
A V(6) log will be added to record requests that are not proxied (i.e., explicitly allowed via NO_PROXY). This helps verify that allowlist rules are functioning as expected.
Rename pkg/probe/http/http.go to pkg/probe/http/http_prober.go: Rename this file to prevent a logging conflict with the file mentioned above, which is the actual target for our enhanced logging.
Why is this needed?
Downstream distributions of Kubernetes, such as GKE, are implementing security features to strictly control and block all egress traffic originating from the kube-apiserver. A core part of this mechanism involves using HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY environment variables to route traffic through a controlled gateway or a "blackhole" proxy, while using a NO_PROXY variable to allowlist essential cluster endpoints.
To safely roll out such a feature, it is critical to have a data-driven way to discover and audit all outbound requests made by the kube-apiserver and other components. This allows operators to build a comprehensive NO_PROXY allowlist and ensure no critical functions are broken. The proposed verbose logging in net/http.go provides this essential visibility.
The second change—renaming pkg/probe/http/http.go—is necessary to avoid unintended log spam. The klog output strips the full file path, so both staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/net/http.go (our target) and pkg/probe/http/http.go (an unrelated file) show up in logs simply as http.go.
As a result, setting --vmodule=http*=5 to enable our new logs also enables verbose logging in the probe helpers, flooding the logs with messages from liveness and readiness probes. This makes it extremely difficult to isolate the critical egress traffic data needed for validation. Renaming the probe helper file to http_prober.go cleanly resolves this name collision and allows for precise, targeted logging for this important security use case.

annotation into account. This leads to an imbalance where two pods with different
pod-template-hash

[TITLE] Kubelet developer on-boarding / component conventions docs [BODY] There are a couple gaps that are closely related and entangled with one another:
How do I make the right kind of changes at a higher level than Go coding guidelines?
How do I approach some component of the system and learn the code effectively?
I originally brought this topic up in the sig-node meeting on Mar 15 and was encouraged to write up an issue with a wider scope by
@dchen1107
.  Hence, my examples are Kubelet-focused.
Let me present as a case study some analysis I did during a recent flake-busting run on the pod IP via env var flake.  The TLDR of that tale is that the existing code was just wrong in the sense that coding conventions in the kubelet were not followed.  In this specific case, the status field in a pod pointer, which should have been read-only, was used to hold the value of the pod IP and was sometimes not set.  The issue was fixed by making the code project-conventional, ie, using the existing internal status management subsystem of the kubelet to get this value where it was needed.
In hindsight, this example seems 20/20 to me as a case where concern (1) above is in play - how do I easily learn the 'way' without necessarily following every single issue and maintaining a mental model of what the current conventions for a component are?  This is not a problem unique to our project, of course, but we should try to have some basic first principles outlined for broad functional areas, at the coarsest possible level of detail to be meaningful without requiring constant update.
Rewinding this story a little to before the fix was determined, debugging the code was pretty instructive for me about learning the code.  I've spent a bit of time in the Kubelet, and yet tracing the Kubelet code and understanding the dependencies of that component was still quite a task.  As it happens, there are around 20 fields of the Kubelet named
*Manager
,
*Cache
,
*Queue
,
*Channel
, etc.  Here is where concern (2) is in play.
These direct dependencies of the Kubelet represent the actors, subsystems, and internal message buses that one has to know in order to reason correctly about the change.  So, in the case of the Kubelet, it might be helpful to have a map-like document of dependencies that describes their roles very concisely, and some behavioral diagrams that show interactions in main code paths like the sync loop.
In the sig node discussion that prompted this issue, we had a loose consensus that something should be done, but also that refactoring efforts shouldn't block on it.  Additionally, it was noted that this type of doc isn't a one-time thing to do, but something that takes maintenance and upkeep.  My personal opinion is that these two factors support that these docs should intentionally be not extensive, and contain as few details as possible while being concise.

[TITLE] ContainerLogManager to rotate logs of all containers in case of disk pressure on host [BODY] What would you like to be added?
The
ContainerLogManager
, responsible for log rotation and cleanup of log files of containers should also rotate logs of all containers in case of disk pressure on host.
Why is this needed?
It often happens that the containers generating heavy log data have compressed log file with size exceeding the containerLogMaxSize limit set in kubelet config.
For example, kubelet has
containerLogMaxSize = 200M
containerLogMaxFiles = 6
Spec 1
Continuously generating 10Mib with 0.1 sec sleep in between
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: generate-huge-logs
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: log-generator
        image: busybox
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
        args:
          - |
            # Generate huge log entries to stdout
            start_time=$(date +%s)
            log_size=0
            target_size=$((4 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024))  # 4 GB target size in bytes
            while [ $log_size -lt $target_size ]; do
              # Generate 1 MB of random data and write it to stdout
              echo "Generating huge log entry at $(date) - $(dd if=/dev/urandom bs=10M count=1 2>/dev/null)"
              log_size=$(($log_size + 1048576))  # Increment size by 1MB
              sleep 0.1  # Sleep to control log generation speed
            done
            end_time=$(date +%s)
            echo "Log generation completed in $((end_time - start_time)) seconds"
      restartPolicy: Never
  backoffLimit: 4

[TITLE] kube-log-runner: avoid torn log records when using log rotation [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Kubernetes components are careful to write all log records with a single write call, which then hopefully translates into a single system call. When passing that output through kube-log-runner with
-log-file-size non-zero
(added in
#127667
), kube-log-runner will split the stream of bytes without considering log record boundaries.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/compare/master...pohly:kubernetes:log-runner-torn-writes?expand=1
demonstrates the problem.
If kube-log-runner were to use Unix Domain
sequential packet sockets
for redirecting the command's output, each write syscall of the command turns into a datagram which can be received completely by kube-log-runner.
/sig instrumentation
cc
@zylxjtu

Ensure that each log file contains complete log records.

[TITLE] Enhancement: Add vTPM Configuration Fields for Enhanced Container Security [BODY] What would you like to be added?
I propose the addition of a new configuration field in Kubernetes to facilitate the creation and mapping of
vTPM
(Virtual Trusted Platform Module) devices into containers. Specifically, the following field should be introduced:
vtpmIdentifier: "/dev/tpm0"
Here, vtpmIdentifier signifies the name of the vTPM device intended to be created. Upon configuring this field, the container platform should instantiate the specified vTPM device and make it accessible within the container.
This proposition aligns with previous efforts by
stefanberger
in the
runc
community, where a vTPM-supporting patch was proposed but not merged into the main branch of runc. (
https://github.com/stefanberger/runc/tree/vtpm
)
As an applied example, alongside creating and mapping the vTPM, introducing an optional
trustedBoot
flag for containers could indicate whether to enable trusted boot functionality, thereby significantly bolstering container security.
Why is this needed?
This enhancement is crucial for container security. Integrating vTPM support bolsters container security by enabling trusted boot processes. Trusted boot ensures the integrity of the boot process, preventing unauthorized modifications and enhancing the overall security posture of containerized applications. With cyber threats on the rise, this feature becomes imperative for protecting sensitive workloads, especially in regulated industries or environments handling confidential data. By integrating vTPM configuration options directly into Kubernetes, we empower users to easily adopt advanced security measures, fostering trust in container deployments and advancing the ecosystem's security standards.

[TITLE] Feature request: parse-able error stream content when port forwarding [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Parse-able error stream content when port forwarding
Why is this needed?
Client-go's PortForwarder
reads from the error stream
, and if anything is received, it
terminates the listener and exits
Often times the error stream will contain a message like
connection refused
or
network namespace for sandbox "ba380ea22e0a0f92d2977c9a56ce03cfc0bafe90e77b284ed297d9d5c8db7e14" is closed
if the pod terminates or otherwise becomes unreachable:
error forwarding port 5432 to pod 8df2641c23fa6d81b236694874f782796c5d17390071bf7202a390da2c776f44, uid : failed to execute portforward in network namespace "/var/run/netns/cni-6311fb2d-d90b-fb84-ba8b-79d627252113": failed to connect to localhost:5432 inside namespace "8df2641c23fa6d81b236694874f782796c5d17390071bf7202a390da2c776f44", IPv4: dial tcp4 127.0.0.1:5432: connect: connection refused IPv6 dial tcp6 [::1]:5432: connect: connection refused
error forwarding port 5432 to pod ba380ea22e0a0f92d2977c9a56ce03cfc0bafe90e77b284ed297d9d5c8db7e14, uid : network namespace for sandbox "ba380ea22e0a0f92d2977c9a56ce03cfc0bafe90e77b284ed297d9d5c8db7e14" is closed
In these cases, it is the correct action for PortForwarder to terminate its listener and exit because the pod is unable to accept and handle new connections.
Other times however, the error stream will contain something that is non-fatal, like
connection reset by peer
, in which case the pod is still running and is still able to accept new connections:
error forwarding port 5432 to pod 8df2641c23fa6d81b236694874f782796c5d17390071bf7202a390da2c776f44, uid : failed to execute portforward in network namespace "/var/run/netns/cni-6311fb2d-d90b-fb84-ba8b-79d627252113": read tcp4 127.0.0.1:43802->127.0.0.1:5432: read: connection reset by peer
In this situation, it is undesirable for PortForwarder to terminate.
In fact this
causes a problem when using psql connected to a postgres instance using SSL
. Postgres issues an ECONNRESET whenever the user who is connected using SSL changes to a different database (using the
\c foo
command for example).
My first instinct was that Client-go's PortForwarder should read what is coming on the error stream, do some kind of regex or other matching, and if it is something non-fatal like "connection reset by peer", then do not terminate the listener. But this isn't a good approach because it relies on the string being written by the container runtime to be a specific string, and for it to be consistent across all container runtimes. It is too fragile.
What if the container runtime can write to the error stream in a consistent and structured way, such as a specific JSON format?
Then, client-go can parse the message and decide what to do for each type of error. The exact format doesn't matter, but here is an example of what I'm thinking:
Old error stream content:
error forwarding port 5432 to pod 8df2641c23fa6d81b236694874f782796c5d17390071bf7202a390da2c776f44, uid : failed to execute portforward in network namespace "/var/run/netns/cni-6311fb2d-d90b-fb84-ba8b-79d627252113": read tcp4 127.0.0.1:43802->127.0.0.1:5432: read: connection reset by peer

{

[TITLE] Not able join worker node to master node upgraded from v1.25.9 to v1.27.1 [BODY] What happened?
Recently, I have upgraded cluster from v1.25.9 to v1.27.1 with CRI-O. While joining new node to M1 using kubeadm, Kubelet.crt is not getting generated which in turn is resulting in auto-restart of kubelet service and the node is not able to join the cluster.
The error is as follows:
Unfortunately, an error has occurred:
timed out waiting for the condition
This error is likely caused by:
The kubelet is not running
The kubelet is unhealthy due to a misconfiguration of the node in some way (required cgroups disabled)
If you are on a systemd-powered system, you can try to troubleshoot the error with the following commands:
'systemctl status kubelet'
'journalctl -xeu kubelet'
I have set systemd cgroup in both config.yaml & crio.conf.
OS version:
CentOS 7

[TITLE] Link to docs from API field descriptions [BODY] The api in v2 has this comment:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/api/v1beta2/types.go
"image pull policy: one of PullAlways, PullNever, PullIfNotPresent; defaults to PullAlways if :latest tag is specified, or PullIfNotPresent otherwise"
this was removed in the v3 types.go file
There's a partial explanation here, but it doesn't specify all possible values:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/docs/images.md
So a documentation for all possible values and the default value is needed.
Also, when working with v1beta1 api, when creating a pod with guestbook examples that don't specify the image pull policy, that property is returned with empty value  "imagePullPolicy": "", shouldn't a default value be populated?

[TITLE] Scheduler: Make sure handlers have synced before scheduling [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Make sure handlers have finished syncing before the scheduling cycles start.
Ref:
#113763 (comment)
/sig scheduling
/good-first-issue
Why is this needed?
In a highly used cluster, we don't want to start scheduling pods before all the pods have been loaded into the scheduler cache, or we could end up in a bad state.

[TITLE] Scheduler incorrectly leaving pods in the unschedulable on node update events [BODY] What happened?
We have an e2e test that involves cluster autoscaler; the test creates two pods back to back which forces CA to scale up the cluster to create two nodes also back to back one for each pod. The two nodes are not created at the same time, there is some delay between them.
The problem is that the second pod never gets scheduled. We see in the logs a single scheduling attempt for the second pod that attempted to schedule it on the first node and failed because it didn't fit the node's remaining cpu cores. We don't see any attempts after that for the pod and the test times out waiting for that pod to schedule.
What changed in the scheduler:
Pre 1.22, on most update/add/delete events to pods/nodes/pvc/storageClass resources, we used to move all unschedulable pods back to the queue. Also every
60 seconds
we did force move all unschedulable pods back to the queue indiscriminately. This behavior is not efficient, wasted scheduling cycles and since we re-queue based on last scheduling attempt timestamp, it missed up badly with the best effort FIFO behavior we intend to have for pod scheduling.
Since 1.22 a couple of things changed such that unschedulable pods are not placed back into the queue on those events indiscriminately; on each such event, we iterate over unschedulable pods and we place them back into the queue if they pass two checks:
the first one happens only on node update/add events, it is carried by the function
preCheckForNode
; it basically runs the kubelet admission logic (node resource, affinity, taints/tolerations and host port checks)
the second check runs on all events (including the node ones); this one is a little more complicated and fine grained: for each unschedulable pod we remember which plugins last failed to fit the pod; at the same time plugins register which events could make an unschedulable pod schedulable (e.g. nodeResources filter plugin registers pod delete and node add/update events). A pod is put back into the queue only if the event matches any of the ones registered by the plugins that last failed the pod.
In 1.24 we increased the 60s to
5min
(our north star to completely remove this)
What went wrong:
My theory is that we incorrectly determined that the pod was not eligible to be put back into the queue on events related to the new node; and that the 5min timeout was too long to force moving it back to the queue (I am guessing the whole test timed out), while the 60s was basically masking the problem for 1.22 and 1.23.
So what checks are incorrectly failing to move the pod? Here is what happened:
Before adding the new node, the pod failed the nodeResource plugin, which only registers for
pod delete, node add and node update allocatable events
New node was added, scheduler receives an add event. The pod was not moved back to the queue because it failed the
preCheckForNode
check on NotReady taint.
When the new node became ready, the scheduler receives a node update event, but since it is a taint update event, it didn't match the events that the nodeResources plugin registered for.
How to fix it:
Since we have the
preCheckForNode
; pods that previously failed because of NodeResources, NodePorts, TaintsAndTolerations and NodeAffinity (the predicates we already ran in
preCheckForNode
) should always be placed back into the queue; basically those plugins should register for all node update events.

[TITLE] [KMSv2] Replace DEK seed cache with non-expiring LRU cache [BODY] /kind feature
/kind cleanup
/sig auth
Previously since >= 1.29, we have promoted the feature gate
KMSv2KDF
to GA and currently the KDF enablement is locked to true via:
kubernetes/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/encryptionconfig/config.go
Lines 128 to 130
      in
05a5960
// this function should be used to determine enablement of the KMSv2KDF feature
// instead of getting it from DefaultFeatureGate as the feature gate is now locked
// to true starting with v1.29
With the KDF feature on, the cardinality of the cache for holding DEK seeds should be low and stable (unless the kube-apiserver keeps re-generating DEK seeds in pathological cases), so far most of the clusters we have seen have lower than 50 DEK seeds in the cache even though the cluster has been running for many years.
Hence, we can consider replace the current expiring cache implementation with
non-expiring LRU cache
(e.g. with 1024 size) so that we don't need to rotate the cache on a day basis --- this helps improving the cluster's resilience to KMS service failures, say the KMS service is down for 5 minutes and if the cluster happens to rotate the cache during the time, it will result in unavailability drop unnecessarily.
Additionally, we can also consider pruning all the occurrences of
useSeed
checks from KMSv2 provider as it's no longer used.

[TITLE] Memory manager and CPU manager state file is not updated immediately when a guaranteed pod is deleted [BODY] What happened?
For guaranteed pod, when Memory Manager/CPU Manager are enabled there are entries in /var/lib/kubelet/memory_manager_state and /var/lib/kubelet/cpu_manager_state that are created capturing the resource allocations per NUMA.
When the pod is deleted the entries in these files are not deleted till a new pod is deployed. Looking at the code, these entries are deleted only when new entries are added as part of pod deployment as part of removeStaleState() where garbage collection happens.
Is this by design?
What did you expect to happen?
Entries in /var/lib/kubelet memory_manager_state and cpu_manager_state files are correctly updated on pod delete.
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Deployed a guaranteed pod with CPU and memory resources specified. CPU manager and Memory manager configured
Using following options in kubelet configuration
--cpu-manager-policy=static --topology-manager-policy=restricted --topology-manager-scope=pod --pod-max-pids=4096 --memory-manager-policy=Static --reserved-memory=0:memory=1024Mi --kube-reserved=memory=462Mi --system-reserved=memory=462Mi
Anything else we need to know?
By adding following change in PostStopContainer() as part of container lifecycle I am seeing the expected behavior. Is it a safe change or was there a reason to not add the cleanup as part of pod deletes. The only reason cleanup is not performed as part of delete would be to reduce the lock contention updating the state files. Is that right?

[TITLE] device manager: potential Double-Locking of Mutex [BODY] What happened?
In the file
pod_devices.go
, there is a potential issue of double-locking a mutex in the function
podDevices
.
In line
102
, the read lock (
pdev.RLock()
) is acquired in the
podDevices
function to ensure safe access to
pdev.devs
.
Later, on line
107
,
podDevices
calls
containerDevices
, which also attempts to acquire the same read lock via another call to
pdev.RLock()
on line
115
. This may result in double-locking the same mutex within the same thread.
Even though both
podDevices
and
containerDevices
only use read locks (
RLock()
), double-locking a mutex, even for reads, can lead to deadlocks, if there is another routine trying to acquire
Lock()
in between the
RLock()
s, according to the documentation of
RWMutex
.
The standard
sync.Mutex()
in
Go
is not a recursive locking implementation while it is used recursively in the
podDevices
function. You can read more on why go does not implement recursive locking
here
.
What did you expect to happen?
The expectation is that a mutex should not be double-locked within the same thread. In this case, either the locking logic needs to be restructured to prevent multiple acquisitions of the same lock or
containerDevices
should not attempt to lock the mutex if it is already locked by
podDevices
.
How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
This issue is identified through static analysis, so it cannot be directly reproduced via runtime observation. However, if left unresolved, it could lead to unpredictable behavior in environments where recursive read locks are not supported.

[TITLE] Scheduler: Sort scheduling failure msgs to better analysis the reason why this node cannot afford pod [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Currently，the scheduling failure msgs from filter stage are as follows, where they are simply sorted by
sort.Strings()
.
0/8 nodes are available: 1 {out-of-tree-plugin-2 reason-2}, 2 Insufficient cpu, 2 {out-of-tree-plugin-1 reason-1}, 2 node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints, 3 Insufficient memory.
I want to sort the failure messages in the order of plugins in the filter stage of the profile.
Example:
- schedulerName: test-scheduler
        plugins:
          ...
          filter:
            enabled:
            - name: out-of-tree-plugin-1
            - name: out-of-tree-plugin-2
         ...
Then, the expected failure msgs are as follows:
0/8 nodes are available: 2 Insufficient cpu, 3 Insufficient memory, 2 node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints, 2 {out-of-tree-plugin-1 reason-1}, 1 {out-of-tree-plugin-2 reason-2}.
Why is this needed?
After sorting the scheduling failure msgs according to the method proposed above, it is more convenient for us to investigate
the reason why a node cannot afford the pod accurately
without increasing the output information.
Because we can determine the specific reason why the node cannot afford the pod one by one in the order of error messages, and we don't know which error message to start checking from before.
Example:
if nodeA can not pass the both
out-of-tree-plugin-2
and
NodeResourcesFit
plugins,  with the previous msgs:
0/8 nodes are available: 1 {out-of-tree-plugin-2 reason-2}, 2 Insufficient cpu, 2 {out-of-tree-plugin-1 reason-1}, 2 node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints, 3 Insufficient memory.
if we check the reason
{out-of-tree-plugin-2 reason-2}
before
Insufficient cpu
for nodeA (Due to we do not known which reason to check firstly), then we may mistakenly believe that the scheduling failure was caused by
reason-2
, rather than
Insufficient cpu
. While it actually caused by
Insufficient cpu
in this scheduling cycle.
After we using following proposed failure msgs:
0/8 nodes are available: 2 Insufficient cpu, 3 Insufficient memory, 2 node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints, 2 {out-of-tree-plugin-1 reason-1}, 1 {out-of-tree-plugin-2 reason-2}.
we can check failure reason  in the order mentioned above, and get the correct failure reason
Insufficient cpu
for nodeA in this scheduling cycle.
Besides, when we have this proposed order of error messages, we can also quickly identify the
failure reasonA
for the node, as it can avoid many unnecessary checks for the reason sorted after
failure reasonA
.

[TITLE] [cloud-provider]: call "EnsureLoadBalancer" method on nodes' labels update [BODY] What would you like to be added?
This is a feature request followup for the
#131085
PR.
Our use case is to use labels selector annotation in lbaas service to include only specific nodes as members of the service (see
kubernetes/cloud-provider-openstack#2601
for implementation details).
E.g.
loadbalancer.openstack.org/node-selector=env=production,az=az1
should configure loadbalancer pool members to use only nodes that have
env=production
and
az=az1
labels.
Unfortunately modifying the node labels doesn't trigger the
EnsureLoadBalancer
cloud controller method, and the only solution is to modify the service spec to add some noop data.
The idea is to modify the
shouldSyncUpdatedNode
cloud-controller func to return true on nodes' labels update:
https://github.com/kubernetes/cloud-provider/blob/ae76f69e43a855438aab6bf3e0ddc3df197b35dd/controllers/service/controller.go#L693-L711
Proposed patch:
diff --git a/controllers/service/controller.go b/controllers/service/controller.go
index 97764cb..0505303 100644
--- a/controllers/service/controller.go
+++ b/controllers/service/controller.go
@@ -26,6 +26,7 @@
import (
        "time"
 
        v1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
+
apiequality "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/equality"
apierrors "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/errors"
        "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/labels"
        "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/runtime"
@@ -706,6 +707,10 @@
func shouldSyncUpdatedNode(oldNode, newNode *v1.Node) bool {
        if oldNode.Spec.ProviderID != newNode.Spec.ProviderID {
                return true
        }
+
// Check if nodes' labels have changed
+
if !apiequality.Semantic.DeepEqual(oldNode.Labels, newNode.Labels) {
+
return true
+
}
return false
 }
This is the last week to prepare for the code freeze. I hope we can introduce this feature into 1.34.
cc
@elmiko
@bowei
@cheftako
@JoelSpeed
Why is this needed?
This feature enables segregation of Kubernetes worker nodes for services with
externalTrafficPolicy=Local
, excluding unused nodes from load balancer pool members and health checks, and reconciling the corresponding service whenever node labels change.
A deeper issue lies in the way F5 (used by OpenStack Octavia LBaaS) handles pool member health: it marks new members as healthy immediately upon addition to the pool, causing traffic to be forwarded to nodes that are not yet ready. By using node selectors, we can prevent new nodes from being added as pool members until they have actual workloads. Moreover, updating the load balancer when node labels change can be beneficial in other scenarios as well.

[TITLE] Hard to understand why a secret of type kubernetes.io/service-account-token referencing an invalid service account gets deleted [BODY] What happened?
Creating a secret of
type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token
with the
kubernetes.io/service-account.name
annotation pointing to a service account that does not exist yet will return success. Yet a subsequent read after create will fail.
If creating the SA and the secret in correct order and then deleting the SA, the secret is deleted as well.

[TITLE] Taint Tolerance Tied to Pod Disruption Budget Availability [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Add a new field to tolerations API to ensure that the PDBs are honored while deleting pods during Taint Based Evictions
Why is this needed?
The current approach of using tolerationSeconds in pod specifications has two key limitations:
Most application developers and cluster operators lack the detailed knowledge required to set tolerationSeconds accurately, leading to guesswork and potential issues. Some clusters have had to implement validating webhooks to prevent indefinite tolerations.
Taint-based "evictions" ultimately result in
pod deletion
, but some workloads require stronger disruption handling guarantees. Cluster admins and developers have had to write custom webhooks to intercept these deletion requests.
To address these challenges, we propose introducing a new field in the Tolerations API called runAsLongAsPDB (or a similar name). This new field would allow users to express their intent to run the workload as long as the Pod Disruption Budget (PDB) exists, eliminating the need for guesswork around tolerationSeconds and providing better disruption handling guarantees. This new functionality would be designed to be backward-compatible with the existing tolerationSeconds approach, allowing both new and existing workloads to benefit from the improved disruption management capabilities

[TITLE] Unclear docs regarding AWS EBS persistent volumes on a Multi AZ cluster [BODY] Hi,
The docs mention that the volume must be created in the same AZ of the cluster.
What happens when I have a multi AZ cluster and make a PVC on a pod for a volume that was created on AZ-X? The docs doesn't mention anything about that.
As I see it there are two options:
The scheduler will be aware of that PVC and schedule that pod only on nodes that belong to AZ-X
The scheduler will not be aware of that and when it schedules the pod to a node on a different AZ than AZ-X the pod creation will fail.
Which of them is the expected behavior?

[TITLE] [Swap Feature] Investigate what happens if a cluster has some swap enabled nodes and others that are not enabled. [BODY] What would you like to be added?
In GA of swap, our goal would be that users/admins can enable swap for their nodes. It could be possible to have a heterogenous cluster where some nodes have swap enabled and others do not.
If a user submits a burstable workload with LimitedSwap, then we would expect swap to be used if feature is on. But if the node does not have swap enabled, then this would not be enabled.
Why is this needed?
This could cause problems with scheduling.
We should investigate and see if there is ways to control this on a heterogeneous cluster.

[TITLE] Improve IP protocol detection on kube-proxy [BODY] What would you like to be added?
As part of the implementation of Dual Stack and also the new nftables backend, kube-proxy now does a validation if IPv4 and IPv6 can be used, for instance
kubernetes/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_linux.go
Line 112
      in
88dfcb2
if
isIPTablesBased
(
s
.
Config
.
Mode
) {
The improvement here is that while kube-proxy does check if IPTables support IPv6 (and nftables is right now hardcoded, but with a pending action), it doesn't really check if IPv4 and IPv6 kernel subsystem are enabled on the operational system.
So before taking the action of checking the filter service support, I would like to propose that we do a check, on Linux, if "/proc/sys/net/ipv4" exists and if "/proc/sys/net/ipv6" exists before moving on to the specific IPtables and nftables checks
One example of the implementation can be found at
rikatz@
6c72306
, tho this implementation doesn't use the filesystem list, but instead the utilsysctl, which may not be ideal in this case
Why is this needed?
Some very specific Linux distributions don't load all the iptables or nftables modules by default, and also don't have auto load (x_tables) working properly due to restrictions and modifications made to work.
Some other distributions disable IPv6 during boot time with ipv6.disable=true. Generally disabling IPv6 doesn't mean the IPv6 rules cannot be added, but on some very specific cases that I could't define why, not all IPv6 filter modules are compiled to the kernel and will partially fail during IPv6 apply, blocking kube-proxy to work.
This is more a proposal to be early defensive on these cases

[TITLE] Allow non secure http access for pulling images from selfhosted private docker registeries [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Current Behavior
If you're using a self-hosted registry (preferably
Docker's official registry
), you may run into an issue where a pod refuses to pull an image unless the registry connection is secured via HTTPS. The only exception is when the registry's domain is localhost.
For example, using:
image: my.path.within.cluster.local:5000/image:latest
won't work because Kubernetes rejects unsecured HTTP connections by default.
Feature Request
It would be helpful to allow defining the protocol explicitly, like this:
image: http://my.path.within.cluster.local:5000/image:latest
or
image:  my.path.within.cluster.local:5000/image:latest
protocol: http
Why is this needed?
This would enable HTTP connections when specified, eliminating the hassle of setting up a local CA just to use an internal registry.
Thanks for considering this!

[TITLE] PowerShell kubectl completion example should dot-source & quote completion script [BODY] The PowerShell example in the
kubectl completion
docs uses a plain path to the
completion.ps1
script when adding to user's profile script. This invokes the script via the
call operator
(
&
) by default and runs in a child scope. The kubectl completion setup in the child scope is lost immediately after the script's execution and provides no benefit to the parent/user scope.
Additionally, the path to the
completion.ps1
script when written to the PowerShell profile with
Add-Content
isn’t quoted. This could raise an issue with some user's
$HOME
paths containing spaces (i.e.
C:/Users/Full Name/
), which would prevent the script from loading properly.
kubernetes/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/completion/completion.go
Lines 103 to 106
      in
b067e45

Add-Content $PROFILE "$HOME\.kube\completion.ps1"
#
Powershell Profile - After running Add-Content ...
C:\Users\Full Name\.kube\completion.ps1
A solution is to use the
dot source operator
(
.
) when executing the script to ensure it runs in the local scope and to quote the full path to the
completion.ps1
script.

The node e2e test suite was written before the component config APIs existed, and so right now the only way to configure a kubelet for tests is with extra command line flags, passed through our current test harness. It would be much better to refactor to just support a custom KubeletConfiguration provided at launch time.
Suggested path forward:
Update our test runner such that we can provide a KubeletConfiguration file, rather than configuring jobs with command-line flags
Determine some mechanism to either update the config and restart the kubelet during test runs, or guidelines for how to manage custom KubeletConfigs in test jobs that need to exercise features outside of the default set
Remove all use of the DynamicKubeletConfiguration from e2e tests

Current Situation
Currently, there are mechanisms like readinessGates that provide control over when a pod is ready to serve external traffic. However, this requires additional specific configurations and does not seem very convenient to use.
Proposal
Can we implement a controller similar to the successPolicy strategy used in Jobs? For example, defining how many replicas under the controller must be ready before the pods can serve external traffic, thereby addressing the load imbalance caused by sequential startup.
Alternatively, are there other approaches that could meet this need?
Why is this needed?
Support rules for defining when controller replicas become available

kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total
metric is only created when the first error occurs. If a kubelet has never encountered a runtime operation error, the metric is absent from the
/metrics
endpoint.
This causes false positive alerts in monitoring systems that track metric absence. Our SLO alerting (using Pyrra) triggers pages when either
kubelet_runtime_operations_total
or
kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total
is missing:
absent(kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total{job="kubelet"}) == 1

kubelet_runtime_operations_errors_total
counter should be initialized to 0 at startup, ensuring it's always present in the metrics output even when no errors have occurred.
Why is this needed?
Prometheus counters should be initialized to 0 to ensure consistent presence.
Missing metrics trigger false alerts in SLO monitoring, especially on stable nodes that rarely encounter errors.

[TITLE] dependencies: hide test-only dependencies from consumers [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Unit tests in our staging repos have the effect that test-only dependencies (such as testify, Gomega, go-spew) are inherited by all downstream consumers importing our staging repos.
We could:
Publish staging repos after stripping out all
*_test.go
files and a
go mod tidy
. This would work. Those consumers who
do
want access to our tests, for example because they run them with different dependencies in their own projects, cannot use our tests anymore. This is a rare use case, but it is done, so this option isn't viable.
For each tag we could publish the same source code without tests, using a
semver tag
with a suffix like
notests
which sorts before the actual tag. Using those alternative tags would have to be an explicit choice. This approach fails as soon as some shared dependencies depends on the normal tag because the the minimal version selection will pick the source code with tests. Reversing the ordering has the same problem.
For each tag we could publish a
<tag>-notests
branch
without the tests. Users could switch to that branch by selecting it explicitly. While this side-steps the minimal version selection problem, it also makes dependency management non-standard. Probably not worth it.
This captures discussions at KubeCon NA 2025. There's no good solution, so unless someone comes up with something better we should close this issue and use it as future reference for why we are publishing tests the way we do.
/cc
@dims
@liggitt
Why is this needed?
Hide dependencies and false vulnerability warnings.

[TITLE] Discussion on Cloud Native Change Management and Control Solutions [BODY] What would you like to be added?
I want to implement cloud-native change management based on K8S. This involves monitoring deployment updates, verifying new pod versions, and combining cloud-native monitoring components, such as Prometheus, to obtain pod metrics and time-series data. Then, using our own intelligent anomaly detection algorithm, we can detect any anomalies in pod metrics and rollback changes in a timely manner. This process is similar to the deployment of Argo-rollouts, but instead of directly operating on the ReplicaSet extension capability, we want to develop a Workload change control framework to extend change management in the cloud-native domain. We have defined two core CRDs, "ChangeWorkload" and "ChangePod". We have developed our own Operator to sense changes in the cloud-native environment, and a SpringBoot control-side application that returns all verification logic to the Operator application.
Regarding the process, we plan to start with deployment and divide it into the following stages:
Change awareness: When the podTemplate of a deployment changes, it is regarded as a new version online and will be processed.
Pre-change verification: Perform some admission verifications based on a webhook mechanism, providing rule configuration verification capabilities such as time window restrictions, such as not allowing changes at midnight.
Change execution blocking: kubectl rollout pause deployment When the control-side application detects a pod anomaly, the change is blocked directly through the API server.
Post-change verification: Support customized verification after the change is completed.
Change self-healing: Directly call the deployment rollback operation via the API server when a version exception is detected.
Do you have any better ideas for the technical solutions for change management in a cloud-native environment? We welcome any suggestions or feedback.
Why is this needed?
Enhancing the stability of changes in cloud native scenarios.

[TITLE] Dynamic Resource Allocation for Container Startup [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Background:
In certain scenarios, containers require a higher amount of CPU resources during their startup phase to accelerate application initialization. This is particularly useful for reducing startup times and ensuring fast application readiness. However, maintaining high resource allocation throughout the container's lifecycle might not be efficient, especially for business logic that can operate well with lower resource limits. This proposal aims to introduce a dynamic resource allocation mechanism specifically tailored for container startup.
Proposal:
Introduce a new feature in Kubernetes that allows users to define dynamic resource allocations for containers during their startup phase. This feature will enhance the existing resource specification by adding a separate configuration for startup resources. This will enable containers to utilize a higher amount of resources only during the initial startup, ensuring faster application initialization.
Specification:
The proposed configuration will be included in the container's resource specification as follows:
resources:
  startup:
    cpu: 4000m
    memory: 750Mi
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 750Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 750Mi
In this configuration, the startup section defines the resource allocation that the container can use during its startup phase. Once the container becomes ready, it will switch to the resource limits specified in the limits section for ongoing operations.
Benefits:
Faster Application Startup: Containers can take advantage of higher resource allocations during startup, significantly reducing application initialization times.
Efficient Resource Utilization: After startup, containers will operate under specified limits, ensuring efficient utilization of resources during normal operations.
Simplified Configuration: The proposed approach keeps the configuration clear and distinct, allowing developers to fine-tune resource requirements based on startup needs and runtime demands.
Considerations:
Impact on Node Resources: The dynamic allocation approach should consider the potential impact on node resources, ensuring that other pods and applications are not adversely affected.
Implementation Complexity: The implementation will need to manage the transition from startup to regular operation, and ensure that the system gracefully handles changes in resource allocation.
Conclusion:
Introducing dynamic resource allocation for container startup in Kubernetes will address the specific requirement of providing higher resource limits during initialization while maintaining efficient resource utilization during normal operations. This enhancement will benefit applications that require fast startup times without compromising on runtime efficiency.
Why is this needed?
Faster Application Startup: Containers can take advantage of higher resource allocations during startup, significantly reducing application initialization times.
Efficient Resource Utilization: After startup, containers will operate under specified limits, ensuring efficient utilization of resources during normal operations.
Simplified Configuration: The proposed approach keeps the configuration clear and distinct, allowing developers to fine-tune resource requirements based on startup needs and runtime demands.

https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/api/v1beta3/types.go#L778
The metadata itself has important fields such as uid/name, etc, that can be used to distinguish one object from another, but if they are not present, then the client needs to sometimes extract name from labels (if present there at all), and it makes the whole work with pod template more complicated and error prone.
What is the reason for omitempty on metadata (being able not to have mandatory fields), and why is it set like this on pod template?

[TITLE] Feature requests: Support adding label based indexes to apiserver cache [BODY] What would you like to be added?
Support adding label based indexes to apiserver cacher to speed up list and watch requests by labels.
Why is this needed?
Background: Each job of the big data computing engine spark/flink will start a master pod to create/list/watch/delete worker pods, namely the Driver pod of spark and the JobManager pod of flink.
spark:
list:
https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/branch-3.5/resource-managers/kubernetes/core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/scheduler/cluster/k8s/ExecutorPodsPollingSnapshotSource.scala#L77-L92
watch:
https://github.com/apache/spark/blob/branch-3.5/resource-managers/kubernetes/core/src/main/scala/org/apache/spark/scheduler/cluster/k8s/ExecutorPodsWatchSnapshotSource.scala#L63-L67
flink:
list:
https://github.com/apache/flink/blob/master/flink-kubernetes/src/main/java/org/apache/flink/kubernetes/kubeclient/Fabric8FlinkKubeClient.java#L207-L215
watch:
https://github.com/apache/flink/blob/master/flink-kubernetes/src/main/java/org/apache/flink/kubernetes/kubeclient/Fabric8FlinkKubeClient.java#L251-L257
In our production k8s cluster, each cluster may run thousands of spark or flink jobs in parallel (the number of jobs may be roughly the same as the number of nodes, or even higher). We found that this will cause great pressure on the apiserver. The number of pod add events sent by the apiserver to the scheduler per second will not keep up with the speed of pod creation per second, resulting in the scheduling speed not matching the speed of pod creation, resulting in resource waste.
Although
#115918
has added namespace indexes to the cacher's watch function, this function is not so useful in scenarios where a large number of jobs are running in a small number of namespaces. Most events are still sent to each cacheWatcher through the cacher first and then filtered, causing high CPU usage on the apiserver and delays in event delivery.
In fact, each spark and flink job only lists and watches the worker pods of each job through the applicationId label of the job, and does not list and watch the worker pods of other jobs (as we can see from the list/watch code of spark and flink above). This is very similar to the way each pod of daemonsets watches the pod of each node according to spec.nodeName. The number of watchers for these jobs is also comparable to the number of watchers for daemonsets.
Since the apiserver has a watch index of spec.nodeName by default, we also want to add an applicationId index, considering that different scenarios may use different label names. Therefore, we optimized the apiserver to build an index based on certain configurable labels, such as
metadata.labels.app
or
metadata.labels.spark-app-selector
, so that the pod event of each job can query the matching watchers in the cacher's dispatchEvent, without having to broadcast to a large number of unmatched cacheWatchers first and then filter them out by cacheWatcher.
Before implementing this feature, we could only isolate an apiserver for the scheduler to use, and big data jobs or daemonsets would not access this apiserver, so that the number of events received by the scheduler per second could keep up with the number of pods created per second. With this feature, we no longer need to isolate the apiserver separately, and the CPU of the apiserver is also reduced a lot.
